items.title: llm-anthropic 0.31
items.summary: Release: llm-anthropic 0.31 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. I've added them to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: uv tool install llm llm install llm-anthropic llm keys set anthropic # paste key here llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. Tags: llm , anthropic , claude , generative-ai , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.summary: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn. From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran: I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map. what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...] Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps. each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound. The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for. There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location? I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app. And since I had one spare device, I then said: add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far Giving Claude Code ears I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears . Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone. I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket. Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem. I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not. Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun. Tags: projects , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , coding-agents , claude-code , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: ChatGPT Enterprise now available in AWS Marketplace
items.summary: ChatGPT Enterprise is now available through AWS Marketplace, helping organizations simplify procurement through existing AWS purchasing and billing relationships.
items.full_text: Today, ChatGPT Enterprise is available through AWS Marketplace. The listing gives organizations a simpler way to discover, buy, and manage ChatGPT Enterprise using their existing AWS purchasing and billing relationship and to apply eligible spend toward their AWS commitments. More than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week . ChatGPT Enterprise brings that familiar experience to work with ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, Codex, and dots. With ChatGPT Enterprise now available in AWS Marketplace, AWS customers get the same models, features, and functionality available directly from OpenAI, with new features released at the same time. These OpenAI products complement the OpenAI models available in Amazon Bedrock . Developers can build AI applications and agents with OpenAI models in Amazon Bedrock, while teams across the business use ChatGPT Enterprise in their daily work. Organizations can choose the approach that fits their workloads and governance requirements. Eligible customers can also access ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Financial Services through AWS Marketplace. Contact your OpenAI or AWS account team to confirm eligibility and get started with ChatGPT Enterprise through AWS Marketplace here ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

items.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
items.summary: Handshake went from launch to $1B in one year pushing the envelope of specialized data for frontier labs. Our first deep dive into a data lab with specific examples across Finance, Bio, and Alignment
items.full_text: ← The conversations Latent Space Podcast What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team Handshake went from launch to $1B in one year pushing the envelope of specialized data for frontier labs. Our first deep dive into a data lab with specific examples across Finance, Bio, and Alignment Listen to this conversation 164 min Read transcript Watch on YouTube This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score. Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating. Who’s in the room 🟣 AI data business — Garrett Lord, Sahil Bhaiwala and Nishant Ranka open and close the episode on the market for expert data. 🌸 Life sciences — Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller put the gel and brain-tissue tasks on screen. 🟢 Finance — Collin Schweiker and Sahil Bhaiwala take us through Project Falcon and its Excel grader. 🟠 Alignment — Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka follow the agent’s tool calls through the safety simulations. Show notes ATLAS-Finance — Explore the benchmark for agents working across a simulated bank’s inboxes, documents, and financial models. Inside a bank — Handshake traces a separate published deal, Project Osprey, from the client’s email to a grading decision. The deal on screen in our interview is Project Falcon. VIALS sample tasks — Try the scientific image questions, including the gel and brain-tissue tasks from the episode. How Handshake trained a model to read scientific figures — The team describes using intermediate image descriptions to train and evaluate a vision-language model. Timestamps 0:00 Inside Handshake AI 0:39 Garrett, Sahil and Nishant on frontier training data 5:15 How to build a banking environment for an agent 13:07 How frontier labs buy data 15:51 How a lab evaluates a new dataset 20:01 Testing training data on open models 27:38 Where rubrics fall short of expert judgment 31:30 Nick and Jonas introduce the VIALS benchmark 35:52 Reading molecular structures and plasmid maps 43:48 Training vision models to interpret scientific images 47:17 Task one: reading the bands on a gel 50:59 Task two: finding necrosis in brain tissue 55:49 Can Python tools help the model see? 1:02:52 Can biology models improve on their own? 1:06:19 What a biology lab can buy from Handshake 1:12:33 Atlas Finance with Collin and Sahil 1:18:56 Inside a simulated investment bank 1:25:45 Where the agent’s financial model went wrong 1:31:18 How a banker grades the spreadsheet 1:41:12 Penalty traps, dependency gates and partial credit 1:46:41 How an agent gamed the Excel grader 1:48:52 What would make an AI banker useful? 1:54:48 Safety and alignment with Steve and Nishant 1:58:25 CAREBench and the limits of a refusal 2:04:42 How safety feedback reaches model training 2:07:21 When an agent sends the wrong files 2:11:14 A loan application tests fair lending 2:16:09 Designing private benchmarks for enterprises 2:25:37 The leadership team on Handshake’s mission 2:28:36 When enterprises need their own models 2:33:03 The market for compute and expert data 2:39:12 Why labs hold out evaluation tasks 2:43:01 Hiring at Handshake AI Thanks for reading Stay a little ahead of the curve. items.title: Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure
items.summary: Learn how OpenAI’s Control Room tracks model workloads across our research infrastructure and can rapidly stop them when safety or security concerns arise.
items.full_text: As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room. Control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems , and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. It has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down. Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest. Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed. Control Room works by integrating a few systems: the workload , the inference engine , and the centralized Control Room service . The workload is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. We require every research workload that does agentic inference to be associated with an approved safety case . The inference engine , or just engine , is the model itself. You can think of the engine as the brain of the model, running directly on GPUs. A workload normally uses one or more models, which might be running on one or more different inference engines. The same inference engine might be used by more than one different workload. The Control Room service tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. Engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output. Control Room is integrated in the following way: When starting a new job, the workload code requests a new job_id from Control Room. Whenever the workload needs to sample tokens from a model, it makes a request to an inference engine running that model, passing the job_id. The engine requests permission from Control Room to fulfill that request, passing the job_id along to Control Room. Control Room checks whether that job has been terminated, and if so, it denies the inference request. The engine responds to the workload's inference request with a refusal, stopping further model output from being produced for that job. How Control Room works STEP 1 A researcher decides to start a job The process starts with a researcher launching a job—for example, an experiment or an evaluation. The job starts up Job code (or workload code) is owned and run by researchers. Inference engines might be started as part of this job, or standalone engines which are not associated with any particular job might already be running. The job registers with Control Room The workload code requests a job ID, associating the job with an approved safety case. The job itself makes this request. Control Room returns a job ID Control Room records the job and returns its identifier. The workload will attach this same ID to its inference requests. The job requests model output from an inference engine The request includes the job_id . This request is made directly from the workload code and does not pass through Control Room. The engine checks permission Before fulfilling the request, the inference engine asks Control Room whether this job is still authorized to run. Control Room allows the request The job is still authorized, so Control Room grants permission. The inference engine can now fulfill the request. The engine returns model output The model generates a response and the engine sends it back to the research job. The job can use that output and continue its work. Something triggers a decision to stop the job A person or monitoring system tells Control Room to stop this job. Control Room marks its ID as stopped. The workload code remains running. The job can still try to sample model output We do not rely on the workload code to correctly perform a check of whether or not the job is still running. The engine checks permission again The engine asks Control Room for permission to fulfill the new inference request, passing along the same job ID. The next authorization is denied When the engine checks permission again, Control Room denies the stopped job. The engine must refuse the inference request. Model output stops—the job stays The engine returns a refusal instead of model output. The research process may remain alive, and the engine remains available to other authorized jobs. All of our frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a monitor. A monitor is another model which inspects everything that the model-being-trained is doing, and raises an alert if it detects a problem. For example, our recent DNS-related incident ⁠ (opens in a new window) was caught by a monitor. Control Room and our monitoring system are integrated in the following way: If the monitoring system detects a potential issue, depending on the details and severity, the monitoring system may decide to stop the job. In this case, the monitoring system sends a message to Control Room to stop the job, passing the job_id. Control Room records that the job is terminated. Next time the job having that job_id makes an inference request to sample more tokens from any model running on any engine, the request will be denied, stopping further model output. The maximum time between the moment when Control Room receives an instruction to stop a job, and the moment when further progress is no longer possible, is 35 seconds. The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly. Workloads, including experiments, evaluation jobs, etc., are normally owned and operated by researchers or teams of researchers. As a result, workload code changes often, and is not an ideal place to implement critical load-bearing safety protections. Because of this, our implementation is designed to be resilient to buggy or broken workload code. We achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that users are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled. Finally, our system “fails closed”, meaning that the Control Room integration in the engines is configured in such a way that if the Control Room service goes down, either due to a system error or because it is disabled for any other reason, including tampering by a bad actor, then all inference requests will be denied until Control Room resumes normal operation. Fail-closed is rolled out now to all frontier model research workloads, and will finish rolling out across all remaining research workloads over the next few days. Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. We’ll continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. If you want to help build systems for the safe and secure development and deployment of AGI, we're ⁠ hiring ⁠ !

items.title: CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more
items.summary: CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.
items.full_text: For Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of CodeRabbit ⁠ (opens in a new window) , trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work. “The first bottleneck that every company hits as soon as you adopt coding agents is code reviews,” Harjot says. CodeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code. Used by over 20,000 organizations and 150,000+ open-source projects, CodeRabbit helps teams understand, review, and secure code produced by AI agents and decide what is ready to ship. According to CodeRabbit, better price-performance from OpenAI helps it add more AI agents to its reviews and pass the benefits to customers, and Codex ⁠ helps it ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team. The company also uses Daybreak ⁠ to both secure its own stack and its customers’ code . Its latest offering, CodeRabbit Secure, uses Daybreak with Codex models to find and fix vulnerabilities using its security-focused agents . “With each OpenAI model release, especially with the reasoning models, we have seen massive improvements in the capabilities of our product to find issues at scale.” – Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO, CodeRabbit CodeRabbit built its first product with GPT‑3.5 Turbo. Harjot says the arrival of GPT‑4 made the product effective at reviewing code. The company went on to adopt OpenAI o1 and OpenAI o3 early. Because code reviews run asynchronously in the cloud, CodeRabbit could use models that took longer to reason through a problem in exchange for more capable analysis. The team evaluates new models against its own benchmark of known issues. At the time of the interview, Harjot estimated that GPT‑6 Astra ⁠ caught 50% of the issues in that dataset, putting it at the top compared to other models in that benchmark. The benchmark continues to evolve as agents introduce different kinds of mistakes and as fixes reveal problems earlier reviews missed. “The nature of bugs keeps evolving, so does our benchmark as the models get better,” says Harjot. Better price-performance from OpenAI models has helped CodeRabbit move capabilities from research into its product. Harjot points to improvements in model pricing and caching that let the company use more AI, add more subagents, and pass the benefits to customers. When CodeRabbit started, it used one or two subagents for code navigation. Lower-cost models such as GPT‑6 Luna now support more subagents throughout the platform, while models such as GPT‑6 Astra handle planning and orchestration. “Now we are using agents everywhere on the use cases we couldn't even afford in the past,” Harjot says. That expands the validation CodeRabbit can perform and the explanations it can give developers, helping them understand and trust changes they did not write themselves. By using Codex, Harjot says the company has been shipping roughly 20 times more software over the last 6 months without adding engineers . He personally estimates that he pushed 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview. Getting there required more than adopting Codex. Running multiple agents exposed constraints across the development process, from laptop memory and compute to testing, the tools that compile and package software, and dependencies. The team streamlined its release process and reconsidered where human approvals belonged, while using CodeRabbit to automatically ship low-risk changes that didn’t need human intervention. “We had to actually completely rethink the entire software delivery,” Harjot says. The company has also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that triages production incidents, Slack messages, and support tickets. It can return a pull request for the team to review and merge. Harjot sees cloud-based development as a way to reduce local-machine constraints and give teams stronger controls over access and auditing. CodeRabbit uses Codex for work beyond engineering, including managing marketing and operational tasks through code. “We are running the company as code as much as possible,” Harjot says. In marketing, the company manages Google Ads through pull requests. The team opens and merges a request to deploy ads. It also uses a content studio repository where Codex creates slide decks and customer-facing documents. “If you can translate your marketing problems to code problems, you will run 10x faster,” Harjot says. CodeRabbit has run agents in sandbox environments since 2023, cloning repositories and letting agents write code to help perform reviews. More recently, CodeRabbit used OpenAI’s Cyber model through Daybreak to test and secure its own platform. The team used the model for internal penetration testing, probing its own platform for ways an attacker could break in. Harjot says the early access helped CodeRabbit secure its own stack. “We found multiple vulnerabilities, advanced hacks that we could not even imagine could happen,” Harjot says. It has since taken those capabilities to market, helping secure its customers’ code with its latest product, CodeRabbit Secure. Over the past two weeks, the company ran a promotional offer where it covered $1M in free deep scans for their users and found over 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans, all powered by Codex models. Thousands of these vulnerabilities have already been fixed by its customers, helping improve their code security. As background agents begin responding to alerts and incidents without a person initiating every task, Harjot expects teams to need more help deciding which changes to take to completion. Looking ahead, CodeRabbit is expanding toward agentic software development, helping teams validate, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-generated code changes at scale. The opportunity is to help developers stay in control as agents do more of the building, with validation, explanations, and maintenance that keep pace with the code being produced.

items.title: Kuken Industries searches 70 years of drawings in minutes
items.summary: Kuken Industries uses the OpenAI API to search 70 years of cooling tower drawings. Engineers can find the drawing for a repair in 4.5 minutes, down from nearly an hour.
items.full_text: Kuken Industries makes air conditioning and ventilation equipment for large buildings, shopping centers, and factories. It holds one of the largest shares of Japan’s cooling tower market. These towers release heat from circulating water into the air, helping cool everything from large buildings and malls to equipment in data centers. When a cooling tower needs a replacement part, Kuken’s engineers turn to an archive of drawings that spans 70 years of installations. For a newer engineer, finding the right drawing often meant asking an experienced colleague where to look and how to read it. Kuken wanted newer engineers to be able to find those records themselves, learn from the decisions they contain, and spend more time figuring out how to make the repair. Parts made today don’t always fit older cooling towers. Without the original drawing to show what was installed, engineers may have to design and manufacture a replacement from scratch. A search by model or part name can turn up several drawings. Over more than 70 years, Kuken has adapted its equipment to individual customers, so specifications vary by customer and installation date. When the archive was on paper, a search could take half a day. Kuken later digitized the archive, but engineers still had to know which name or number to look up and where to find the file. Newer engineers in particular spent time piecing those details together. Kuken wanted engineers at every experience level to be able to search the archive on their own. As it explored how AI might help, Kuken connected with Recursive, a Japanese AI startup and an official OpenAI partner. The two companies built the search system and its field app together, drawing on Kuken’s archive and input from its engineers. They tested several AI models on a range of drawings to see how accurately each could extract details and at what cost. OpenAI’s models performed well on both measures, and the OpenAI API gave the team the flexibility to build search directly into the app. Conversations with field engineers shaped how the search works. Engineers can enter a drawing or part number, or upload an image or PDF of a drawing or parts list. Pasting in a screenshot of the list saves engineers from entering each number by hand. The app reads the part numbers and returns possible matches, including drawings for similar designs. To find the right drawing, engineers check the tower’s specifications and records of past replacements. Kuken reports the following results from using and testing the search tool. Kuken expects the tool to cut the hours spent searching for drawings by about 90% over a year. Experienced engineers use some of the time they save to mentor newer colleagues. Engineers can review drawings in the app, reducing printing costs. Engineers now spend less time looking for a drawing and more time studying it. Both newer engineers and veterans say that gives them room to consider design improvements and explore ideas they previously had little time to pursue. Newer engineers can now handle a wider range of jobs on their own. Experienced colleagues who used to guide them through each search have more time to teach and to take on engineering work of their own. “People now have time to do work they’ve wanted to try and take on new challenges. That’s been a real source of motivation.” —Takatsugu Naraki, Director and Factory Manager, Kuken Industries Kuken is also developing a tool to check drawings prepared by its partners. Today, engineers compare each drawing with the specifications by eye, looking for details or quantities that don’t match. Kuken wants the tool to flag those differences so engineers can review drawings faster and catch mistakes they might otherwise miss. According to Kuken, in prototype testing, about 90% of the issues the AI flagged were genuine discrepancies. If the tool moves into production, Kuken expects it to substantially reduce the time engineers spend checking drawings. Each drawing records decisions an engineer made for a particular installation. By making those decisions easier to find and understand, Kuken aims to pass that experience on to the next generation of engineers. “I believe OpenAI’s technology can help manufacturers like us pass skills on to the next generation. That’s long been a challenge for us.” —Takatsugu Naraki, Director and Factory Manager, Kuken Industries Join the new era of work More than 1 million businesses around the world are achieving meaningful results with OpenAI.

items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
items.summary: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it <details><summary> or <summary><details> ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the <details> element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) Tags: github , html , markdown , ai , datasette , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-programming , llm , coding-agents

items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.summary: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . Tags: research , c , rust , sqlite , claude

items.title: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
items.summary: What happens when students can one-shot last year’s homework? Inside CS146S and the engineering team at Monaco.
items.full_text:
Automated transcript, aligned to the final episode. Timestamps open the corresponding moment on YouTube. 0:00 swyx · Intro — Okay, this is a pretty special episode because we're celebrating 1 million subscribers on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. So go over there and subscribe if you haven't heard about it. The guest is Mihail Eric, who is not only teaching The Modern Software Developer at Stanford, which is going viral right now, for basically covering all the AI-native development best practices, but also he is head of AI in Monaco. So he's not only a teacher, but he's a practitioner. 0:24 And those of you coming to AI Engineer CODE Summit next week, it's going to be the celebration of all the extreme progress that you've seen in coding in the last year. I'm excited about all the themes of fighting slop, of system one models, and of increasing your ambition for major rewrites of basically everything that you've seen in code. There's never been a more exciting time to be an AI engineer. And with one million AI engineers, I think it's just getting started. 0:49 So let's get into the interview. 0:51 Okay, we're in the studio with Mihail Eric, adjunct professor at Stanford and head of AI at Monaco. Welcome. Thank you. I'm glad to be here. You caught our attention because of your course that you are refreshing for the third time, third time? 1:03 Second time. Second time. Yep. The CS146, or 146S, The Modern Software Developer at Stanford. 1:09 Mihail Eric · EO Studio excerpt — This particular generation of junior developers, of junior engineers, the people that are now entering the workforce, will, I think, be the first kind of generation of that new shift. 1:18 And I looked at the syllabus and I was like, this is everything we cover. So every now and then I like to invite people like yourself who like you cover a broad range of topics and then we can sort of go topic by topic and Give people the state of the art on each of these things, which I assume you're doing with all your guests anyway For sure. Tell us the history of the course. 1:36 What made you want to Spring out CS 146? Yeah, is the second time it's being taught and I I taught it for the first time last fall, so fall 2025. This was pre 4.5, 4.6 days. even before fall 2025, the course had been about a year in the making. The genesis of the class was probably November of 2024. And I had sort of had this idea that we're seeing all this stuff happening in coding agents, and yes, they were an earlier version of the coding agents, but already it felt like there was something drastically changing in terms of how developers were doing their work, quickly we were getting work done, all that fun stuff. 2:08 And so at the time, was all just scattered blog posts, scattered things you could find online if you were trying to get into the methodology of how to do these things. And so I had this idea like, hey, well, is there a way to kind of structure a curriculum around this that's a little bit more formal? 2:23 Had the idea, and my alma mater is Stanford, and I always had this to go back and teach something and kind of pay it forward. I've always been very deep into education. And talked to Chip who also taught a class one of my good friends Chip Yen yeah Chip exactly spoke to her she had taught her I guess designing machine learning systems and so like asked her what that process was like and sort of you know took a lot of inspiration from how she designed the curriculum and thought about you know getting something the school put it together spent about nine to ten months this was now fall of 2024 through to like you know mid to late of 2025 got it through the committee, 2:58 made a case for the class to exist, you know, had to put together a proposal and everything. And that took me to fall 2025 when I heard it for the first time, was very well received. know, students were really interested in it. There was even, I guess, like a Business Insider article that was written about the class last year. And then, yeah, this year, a lot of things changed. I would say really agents, autonomous coding agents, really picked up in a way that we had not seen before. 3:23 So it felt like it was time to do this again, refresh things, and then here we are. Meanwhile, you're also head of AI at Monaco, which is also a very buzzy startup. Yes, yes. We are in the airwaves right now and having a fun time doing it. Yeah, so I do like that you're also, I guess, a practitioner. You guys are obviously implementing all this stuff at Monaco. Yeah. Any, I guess, principles or observations about just have changed from last year to this year at a high level? 3:53 Yeah, yeah. a ton. I think that when I reflect on what last year's version of the class was, I mean, coding agents had been around, but we were still in kind of that phase where companies were emerging that were tackling every single part of, like, the AIS DLC. There was, like, a coding agent for code review. There was a coding agent for spec design. There was a coding agent for SRE. And, you know, some of those, of course, some of those companies still exist. 4:16 But it felt like last year it was a lot more about a broad tour of here's everywhere you can use coding agents. And in a way, a lot of the curriculum last year was geared toward exposure. And this kind of survey, this kind of like odyssey of sorts through, hey, everything that you knew ASDLC is now changing because of AI. This year, I think there's some principles that are solidifying, right? 4:38 The idea of like very careful context engineering, the idea of like really thinking through sort of like design and architecture as a way of handling really complex tasks. And so the nature of my class is it's not intended for the like beginner programmer. That is not a replacement for like traditional computer science in the sense of like algorithms. And if in fact a lot of those classes are prereqs to what I'm doing here. 4:59 But I do know that you have a good foundation, going now toward applying that and sort of using those principles in production environments in the real world, that's something that I think is now at a place where, you know, at Monarcha we deal with massive code bases. You know, I help a lot of companies also with thinking through their massive code base designs and things like that. And so it's more of a practitioner's course for once the students, graduated or now entering the workforce, how to be the most productive members workforce. 5:25 You said you're passionate about education. I feel like students in that phase of being in college are in a pretty interesting spot. any advice and any take should people study computer science right now? 5:40 Is Claude code and codex all we need? Like, I want to, you know, hear your thoughts. Yeah, I, you know, there's a lot of anxiety from students, as you can probably imagine. And I think a lot of what I'm trying to communicate this time around is that the anxiety, a lot of it still is here. And there was anxiety last year as well. But I want to make the case that a well -trained AI native engineer, and I know that's like a buzzy word, but let's say we'll dive into maybe what aspects that are most interesting. 6:10 A well -trained and native engineer can be some of the most useful assets to any company around. 6:17 This is the first week of class, actually. Week one, first lecture, I'm like, hey, I really believe that every company needs you, but the floor is much higher. What do you assign when a coding agent can finish last year’s homework in one prompt? In the second run of Stanford’s CS146S, Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course. Students have to learn an unfamiliar repo, propose a change, and explain the patch to the person who might merge it. We invited Mihail, who teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, to celebrate one million subscribers on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. He opens up the course syllabus and shows us which lessons survived contact with his own engineering team. Monaco built its agent workspaces, bought its code review tools, and gave an on-call agent access to Datadog and GitHub. We ask how he decides which tools his team needs to own. Watch the full interview and screenshares on YouTube . Show notes Timestamps 0:00 One million AI Engineer subscribers and the CODE Summit 0:51 Mihail Eric and Stanford CS146S 5:26 What junior engineers need to learn now 10:02 Open-source maintainers review the students’ code 15:04 A tour of the ten-week syllabus 24:04 The loop, tools and harness inside a coding agent 32:18 Context engineering for a large codebase 38:15 Skills that make you understand the diff 46:42 The Monaco.com dispute and the airplane banner 50:23 What Monaco does for sales teams 59:21 Inside Monaco’s engineering team 1:01:40 “You buy to learn, and you build to keep” 1:05:24 Making repos agent-ready and closing the on-call loop 1:12:37 When code review becomes the bottleneck 1:20:37 Security, dependencies and permissions 1:30:13 Background agents and Stripe’s Minions 1:34:16 MCP portals and why infrastructure converges 1:41:22 Building the software factory 1:45:24 What work is left for developers? 1:52:16 From personal adoption to team autonomy Opening excerpt from The Thinking Mode, EO Studio .

items.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
items.summary: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! Tags: firefox , html , mozilla , datasette

items.title: Terry Pratchett's Study
items.summary: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news , terry-pratchett

items.readme_text:
Kiro Crew

A persistent workspace for development work that self-improves and continues beyond one session.

Kiro Crew is an open source development workspace that runs locally or remotely on your hardware. It is persistent, self-learning, and self-evolving. Work with it from the desktop app, web dashboard, and CLI, or continue the same work through connection tools like Slack and Discord. Your multi-step tasks can run unattended, recurring jobs run on your schedule, and heartbeats monitor systems until something needs attention. Kiro Crew Apps tailor that experience to a specific job, combining a purpose-built interface with agents, skills, schedules, integrations, and backend services.

Quick start · Build from source · Why Kiro Crew · Capabilities · How it works · Security · Install · Telemetry · Docs

## Quick start You choose how to run Kiro Crew: the desktop app with automatic updates, a one-line install on your machine or a remote host, the Docker image for always-on servers, or a build from source. The default agent runs on `kiro-cli`, which you install and sign in to separately. First launch checks that prerequisite and links to the official setup guide when it is missing. ### App downloads Each link fetches the newest build on that channel, and the app then updates itself on the same channel. Take Stable unless you have a reason not to; see [Release channels](#release-channels) below. | Download | Stable | Insider | Nightly | |---|---|---|---| | **macOS** (Apple Silicon/Intel) `.dmg` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew.dmg) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew.dmg) | | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.rpm) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.rpm) | | **Linux** x86_64 in-app updates. The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#installing-a-linux-desktop-package) owns which Linux package to pick, platform requirements, and sandbox setup. ### Release channels Stable is the default; Insider follows release candidates, and Nightly follows `main`. The [release runbook](docs/build/release.md#the-three-channels) owns the current triggers, version shapes, promotion behavior, cadence, and update-lane semantics. ### One-line install Install the signed Stable wheel without cloning the repository or building the frontend: ```bash curl -fsSL https://download.crew.kiro.dev/cli.sh | sh ``` Then open `http://localhost:5476`. Pass `--version` to pin an exact release — the minimum pinnable release is `0.1.2`, because `0.1.0` and `0.1.1` predate manifest signing and have no signed manifest to resolve: ```bash curl -fsSL https://download.crew.kiro.dev/cli.sh | sh -s -- --version 0.6.0 ``` The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#a-one-line-install-fastest) owns channel selection, managed versus system Python, mirrors, first-run setup, upgrades, and recovery. ### Docker For always-on servers, the Gateway ships as a public multi-arch image on GHCR: ```bash docker run -d --name kirocrew \ -p 127.0.0.1:5476:5476 \ -v kirocrew-home:/home/kirocrew \ ghcr.io/kirodotdev/kirocrew:stable ``` See the [Docker guide](docs/guides/docker.md) for first-run login, channel tags, and the container security model. ### Build from source macOS and Linux require Python 3.12+, Node.js 22.12+ (24 LTS recommended), and npm. The default ACP backend also requires [`kiro-cli`](https://kiro.dev/docs/cli/): install it on the Gateway host and run `kiro-cli login` before using that backend. Other verified ACP harnesses have their own prerequisites in the [install guide](docs/guides/install.md). Windows is supported through a native source install; follow the [Windows guide](docs/guides/windows-install.md) instead of the shell steps below. ```bash # 1. Clone and build Kiro Crew git clone https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew.git cd KiroCrew make build source .venv/bin/activate # 2. Configure, verify, and start kirocrew setup kirocrew doctor kirocrew gateway ``` ## Why Kiro Crew Most agent sessions end when the chat closes. Kiro Crew runs continuously on hardware you control and keeps working between conversations. **Persistent.** Sessions, memory, schedules, and task checkpoints survive Gateway restarts, and scheduled or reactive work continues without someone at the terminal. **Self-learning.** Corrections and task failures become durable lessons. Preferences and project context carry into new sessions. **Self-evolving.** Repeated patterns become reusable skills. Memory, lessons, and skills stay visible and editable, so each Kiro Crew grows more tailored to the person and work around it. **Runs where you choose.** Your Mac, a local container, or a remote machine you control. **One Gateway, many surfaces.** Work directly in the desktop app or web dashboard, or continue the same work from the CLI and messaging surfaces like Slack and Discord. ## What Kiro Crew does | Capability | What it gives you | |---|---| | **Persistent sessions** | Run concurrent, isolated conversations, resume them after Gateway restarts, search prior sessions, and carry recent context into new work. | | **Self-learning** | Turn corrections and task failures into durable lessons that change later behavior. Lessons can apply globally or carry a `repo_scope` that limits them to one repository; Crew Members keep private lessons in their own memory store. | | **Self-evolving skills** | Synthesize reusable skills from repeated patterns, then inspect, refine, or remove them as your work changes. | | **Long-running tasks** | Give Kiro Crew a task spec and walk away. It plans steps, executes them, validates results, retries failures, and resumes from checkpoints. *"Implement this migration plan and stop if the tests fail"* runs as a checkpointed task with validation at each step. | | **Unattended autonomy** | Run scheduled agent work or deterministic scripts and commands without a model call. Monitor work until it is done, or react to messaging events and authenticated webhooks without someone at the terminal. *"Every weekday at 9, summarize the open work I should review"* becomes a timezone-aware recurring job delivered to the surface you choose. | | **Delegation** | Spawn isolated subagents for parallel work and bring their results back into the parent conversation. *"Research these three options in parallel and recommend one"* fans out to isolated subagents and synthesizes the tradeoffs. | | **Work where you choose** | Work directly in the desktop app or web dashboard, or continue through the CLI and any connected messaging surface without moving the agent runtime or its state. | | **Installable Apps** | Add focused interfaces and domain workflows through dashboard pages, scoped Gateway APIs, events, and lifecycle hooks. | | **Extensible tools** | Add MCP servers, markdown skills, and hooks without changing the core runtime. | | **Visible execution** | Watch tool calls, subagent progress, context usage, approvals, schedules, memory, and logs from the dashboard. | | **Defense in depth** | Combine tool approvals, OS sandboxing, sensitive-path checks, credential redaction, deny rules, audit events, and governance profiles. | You can also paste a screenshot and ask what is causing an error. Kiro Crew sends the image to the active Kiro model and keeps the diagnosis in the conversation history. The complete inventory is in [Features](src/kiro_crew/docs/index.md) and [What's New](CHANGELOG.md). ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Desktop app · Web dashboard · CLI · Messaging channels"] G["Gateway
access · sessions · memory · schedules · approvals · apps"] A["Agent sessions
ACP runtime · selected harness · MCP tools · models"] S --> G --> A ``` The Gateway separates where the agent runs from where you work. Each conversation or background task is a logical agent session driven through the selected `agent.acp_backend`; depending on that harness and workload, the session uses a dedicated process or a handle on a shared ACP runtime. State, policy, approvals, schedules, memory, and apps remain on the Gateway host. See the [architecture overview](docs/architecture/overview.md) for component boundaries, [sessions](docs/system-specs/modules/session.md) for lifecycle and isolation, and [MCP architecture](docs/architecture/mcp.md) for tool exposure. ## Security and control Kiro Crew enforces approvals, OS isolation where available, sensitive-path and credential guards, denied-operation rules, audit records, and an optional policy/profile ceiling at the runtime boundary. The dashboard binds to loopback by default; any remote exposure requires authenticated configuration. Read the canonical [security model](docs/system-specs/modules/security.md) and [security architecture](docs/architecture/security-deep-dive.md) before changing or widening those controls. Protect credentials, review high-impact actions, and use [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for private vulnerability reporting. ## Install, configure, and operate The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md) owns every install path, first-run step, optional dependency, upgrade, uninstall, and recovery procedure. User data lives under `~/.kiro/crew` by default and moves with `KIROCREW_HOME`; configuration keys and precedence are canonical in the [config spec](docs/system-specs/modules/config.md). For a new source or wheel install: ```bash kirocrew setup kirocrew doctor kirocrew gateway ``` Run the Gateway as a boot-persistent service when needed: ```bash kirocrew service install kirocrew service status kirocrew logs ``` Service ports, systemd/launchd behavior, containers, and remote-host access are documented in the [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#running-as-a-service), [Docker guide](docs/guides/docker.md), and [remote host guide](docs/guides/remote-and-mobile.md). Use `kirocrew config get`, `kirocrew config set `, and `kirocrew config edit` for the main configuration. Set a process port with `KIROCREW_PORT` or `kirocrew gateway --port `. Start troubleshooting with `kirocrew doctor`, then inspect `kirocrew logs` (or `kirocrew logs -f`). See the [troubleshooting guide](src/kiro_crew/docs/troubleshooting.md) for log sources, levels, diagnostics bundles, and recovery steps. ## Anonymous usage telemetry Kiro Crew sends **one anonymous heartbeat per day** so maintainers can see how many copies are actively running and which releases, Python minors, and install paths still need support. After a successful install or update from the official app catalog, it also sends one anonymous per-app receipt. Both signals are enabled by default, but first egress waits until the first-run privacy disclosure has been shown; they use the same controls below. To turn it off, click **Turn off** on the Privacy screen of first-run onboarding, or flip **Settings > Privacy > Send anonymous usage heartbeat** in the dashboard. Or from a terminal: ```bash kirocrew telemetry disable # local metrics and the heartbeat; persists to config.json export KIROCREW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 # heartbeat only, per-shell / per-container export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 # everything: local metrics and the heartbeat kirocrew telemetry status # print both switches and exactly what would be sent ``` Turn off and `kirocrew telemetry disable` write the same settings, so either one sticks across restarts and upgrades. `KIROCREW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` and `DO_NOT_TRACK` override them: when one is set, the dashboard toggle is disabled and says so. When the Privacy screen's text changes, existing users see it once more at their next dashboard load while local recording is on. **Exactly these five fields are sent, at most once per day, and nothing else:** | Field | Example | Why | |-------|---------|-----| | Random instance id | `9c75560d…` (UUID4) | Lets us count how many copies ran on a given day. Generated once on first run and derived from nothing — not your hostname, username, MAC, IP, or any account. It identifies an installed copy, never a person. | | App version | `0.1.2` | Which releases are still in use. **Release number only** — build stamps like `-nightly.20260731t065756` are stripped before sending, because a per-build timestamp is near-unique and would help identify a specific machine. | | Python minor version | `3.12` | When the minimum can move up | | Install path | `dmg` | Which distribution format people actually use | | First-send flag | `1` / `0` | First successfully reported install vs returning | **Official-app install receipts are separate and event-based.** After a successful official-catalog install or update, Kiro Crew sends one GET to `/b/1/install/?t=&k=&v=` on the same telemetry host. The slug is the public catalog identifier. `t` is the first 32 hex characters of HMAC-SHA256 keyed by an independent local receipt secret over `app-install:`; that secret never leaves the machine, so tokens for different apps cannot be linked to each other or to the heartbeat install id. `k` separates fresh installs from updates, and `v` is the same release-only Kiro Crew version clamp used by the heartbeat. Receipts are emitted only for bundled or edition-provided official catalog entries. Apps from user-configured registries, local-directory installs, and self-registered apps emit nothing, so private app names never leave the machine. If the receipt-only secret cannot be persisted, the receipt is skipped. This list used to be nine fields. Release channel, OS, CPU architecture and governance posture were **removed** — each was coarse on its own, but the instance id is stable, so those attributes all describe the *same* copy and together they narrowed the group any one install blends into far more than any single field suggests. We report this as **Daily Active Crews** rather than "users": Kiro Crew has no account system of its own, and the Kiro sign-in that `kiro-cli` uses for model access is never read or sent. There is no way to resolve a copy to a person, so one person running Kiro Crew on three machines counts as three Crews. **Never sent:** your prompts, model responses, file contents, file paths, repo or branch names, credentials, environment variables, hostname, username, or IP address. The receiving CDN is configured **not to log client IP addresses** — the log delivery does not include that field, so no IP is stored at all. **Automatically off** in CI, and whenever `KIROCREW_HOME` points somewhere other than `~/.kiro/crew` (dev instances and pods are never counted). **Enterprise administrators can pin it off entirely.** A `capabilities.telemetry` entry in the security policy blocks both outbound signals regardless of the local setting, and the dashboard toggle then says so instead of offering a change that would not take effect: ```json {"version": 1, "boot": {"fail_closed": true}, "capabilities": {"telemetry": {"enabled": false}}} ``` See [docs/system-specs/modules/governance.md](docs/system-specs/modules/governance.md). This is separate from `telemetry.enabled`, which controls **local-only** performance metrics that never leave your machine. See [docs/system-specs/modules/metrics.md](docs/system-specs/modules/metrics.md). ## Docs and contributing | Topic | Start here | |---|---| | Install and packaging | [Install and build](docs/guides/install.md), [Windows](docs/guides/windows-install.md), [Docker](docs/guides/docker.md), [Desktop](docs/build/desktop-app.md), [Remote host](docs/guides/remote-and-mobile.md), [Release process](docs/build/release.md) | | Product capabilities | [Features](src/kiro_crew/docs/index.md), [Skills](skills/README.md), [All user docs](src/kiro_crew/docs/README.md) | | All documentation | [docs/](docs/README.md) for contributor and architecture docs | | Channels | [Slack](docs/guides/slack-setup.md), [Discord](src/kiro_crew/docs/discord-integration.md), [Telegram](src/kiro_crew/docs/telegram-integration.md), [Teams](src/kiro_crew/docs/teams-integration.md), [Webex](src/kiro_crew/docs/webex-integration.md), [WeCom](src/kiro_crew/docs/wecom-integration.md), [WeChat (Weixin)](src/kiro_crew/docs/weixin-integration.md), [WhatsApp](src/kiro_crew/docs/whatsapp-integration.md), [Feishu (Lark)](src/kiro_crew/docs/feishu-integration.md), [iMessage](src/kiro_crew/docs/imessage-integration.md) | | Architecture | [System architecture](docs/architecture/overview.md), [Memory](docs/system-specs/modules/memory-skills-hooks.md), [MCP](docs/architecture/mcp.md), [App Kit](docs/app-kit/getting-started.md) | | Trust and dependencies | [Security](docs/architecture/security-deep-dive.md), [Security policy](SECURITY.md) | | Project work | [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md), [Tenets](TENETS.md), [Governance](GOVERNANCE.md), [Maintainers](MAINTAINERS.md), [AI assistant rules](AGENTS.md), [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) | Contributions are welcome. Follow [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for setup, change-scoped validation, commit format, and the pull-request workflow. Use [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/issues) for bugs and feature requests; report vulnerabilities privately through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Contributors Kiro Crew was made possible by its internal community, the people who supported the project and shipped its code, together with everyone who has since opened a pull request in the open. This is that founding group; as Kiro Crew grows in the open, we look forward to many more contributors joining them. Thank you to everyone who helped make this tool possible:

items.readme_text:
Cherry Studio Mobile

Your AI workspace on iOS and Android.
Chat with your favorite models, connect your tools, and turn ideas into images.

Features · Development · Documentation · Feedback · Desktop

## A Look Inside

Conversations · Image creation · Connected tools
Real app screenshots captured on iPhone 17 Pro.

## Features ### 💬 Your Models, One Conversation Space Connect multiple AI providers, manage your models, and choose the right one for each conversation. Read streaming responses with Markdown formatting and bring images and text attachments into the conversation, subject to the selected model's capabilities. ### 🍒 Agents That Work Your Way Create agents with their own instructions, default models, and tools. Keep separate conversations for different projects, and review tool actions when approval is required. ### 🔌 Connect Your Tools Extend your agents with plugins and MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers. Search the web and read pages with configured search services. Connected tools become available according to their setup, permissions, and each agent's configuration. ### 🎨 Turn Ideas Into Images Start from a prompt or a visual template, choose an image model, and create something new. Revisit your drawing history and use existing images as the starting point for another creation. ### 📎 Keep And Share Your Work Manage attachments and generated files in the file library. Preview documents and export selected conversation content as Markdown, HTML, or an image, with available formats depending on the selection. ### 📱 Made For Mobile, Connected To Cherry Use light and dark themes, native navigation, and the system share sheet. Pair with Cherry Studio Desktop to import supported provider configurations and models. Conversation history and remote agent control are outside the current pairing feature. Model and connected-service availability depends on your configuration. Some providers require an account or API key and may charge for usage. ## Development Built with Expo and React Native. Use **Node.js 24** and **pnpm 12.2.1**. ```bash pnpm install # Build and install the development client for one platform: pnpm ios # or: pnpm android # Start Metro for an already installed development client: pnpm dev ``` The app includes custom native modules and requires a development client. See the [development guide](docs/guides/development.md) for setup and daily development, and [Local EAS Builds](docs/guides/local-builds.md) for installation packages and app variants. ## Contributing Help shape Cherry Mobile through code, bug reports, product ideas, and documentation. - [Report a bug or suggest a feature](https://github.com/CherryHQ/cherry-studio-app/issues/new/choose) - Read the [Git workflow](docs/guides/git-workflow.md) and [testing guide](docs/guides/testing-and-ci.md) before preparing a pull request. - Explore the [project documentation](docs/README.md) for architecture and development conventions. ## Community Cherry Mobile is part of [Cherry Studio](https://github.com/CherryHQ/cherry-studio). [Official website](https://cherry-ai.com) · [Discord](https://discord.gg/wez8HtpxqQ) · [Telegram](https://t.me/CherryStudioAI) ## License [GNU Affero General Public License v3.0](LICENSE).
