| Block, redact and warn with mock model responses | | [spend_cap](examples/spend_cap/) | Observed-cost budgets with a mock model | | [agent_service](examples/agent_service/) | HTTP service and SSE events | | [scoped_service](examples/scoped_service/) | Offline shared service with owner-scoped sessions and file tools | | [webui](examples/webui/) | Embedded browser UI | | [dingtalk_channel](examples/dingtalk_channel/) | DingTalk messages and confirmations | | [scheduled_task](examples/scheduled_task/) | One-shot and recurring tasks | | [realtime_echo](examples/realtime_echo/) | A realtime-interface echo client | | [edge_offline](examples/edge_offline/) | Cloud/local routing with Ollama | | [edge_sensor](examples/edge_sensor/) | Sensor middleware with a mock sensor | | [edge_serial_robot](examples/edge_serial_robot/) | Device tools with a mock serial device | | [edge_fleet](examples/edge_fleet/) | In-memory pub/sub fleet simulation | | [werewolves](examples/werewolves/) | A multi-agent Werewolves game | | [k8s_workspace](examples/k8s_workspace/) | Kubernetes workspace configuration and cluster tools |
The [examples guide](docs/examples.md) provides running instructions and links to the same catalog. ## Documentation | Topic | Guide | |---|---| | Setup and a first agent | [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) | | Models and tools | [Providers](docs/model-providers.md) · [Tools](docs/tools.md) | | Context compaction | [Experimental tool-exchange retention](docs/context-compaction.md) | | Managed text tasks | [Fixed-deployment execution, limits and accounting](docs/managed-task.md) · [Routing and deployment pools](docs/managed-routing.md) · [Evaluation workflow](docs/managed-routing-evaluation.md) | | Probabilistic classification | [Classifier API and attempt accounting](docs/classifier.md) · [Jev adapter](docs/jev.md) · [Bailian adapter](docs/bailian.md) · [OpenAI Decisions adapter](docs/openai-decisions.md) | | Middleware and memory | [Middleware](docs/middleware.md) | | Goal execution | [Experimental GoalPipeline and Agent adapters](docs/goal-pipeline.md) | | Named-member teams | [Experimental serial TeamPipeline and host interactions](docs/team-pipeline.md) | | Shared HTTP service | [Experimental owner-scoped sessions and request-aware construction](docs/scoped-service.md) | | Application deployment | [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) · [Execution and session limits](docs/adversarial-hardening.md) · [Reply recovery](docs/reply-recovery.md) | | OpenAI-compatible serving | [Experimental Chat Completions handler and client contract](docs/openai-serving.md) | | Runtime and evaluation | [Runtime features](docs/go-exclusive.md) · [Load and quality testing](docs/benchmarks.md) · [Replay and evaluation source](pkg/agentscope/replay/) | | Local models and devices | [Edge deployment](docs/edge-deployment.md) · [Device tools](docs/device-tools.md) · [Multi-device coordination](docs/multi-device.md) · [Offline operation](docs/offline-operation.md) | | Implementation and compatibility | [Source map](CLAUDE.md) · [API stability](STABILITY.md) · [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) | ## Project status Stability varies by package. The core model, message, agent, tool, permission, formatter and error APIs have documented stability commitments; other packages include experimental interfaces. Read [STABILITY.md](STABILITY.md) for the exact scope and remaining hardening work. Features on `main` may not be in a release. For deployments that execute shell commands or access files, configure and test the appropriate workspace backend and permissions. Permission checks alone do not provide complete process, network or resource isolation. Deployment requirements depend on the selected providers and backends. ## Contributing Bug reports, regression tests, documentation and focused feature contributions are welcome. For a bug, include the version or commit, configuration and a minimal reproduction with secrets removed. For a larger feature, open an issue to discuss the use case and API before starting a broad implementation. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for setup and the PR process, and [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for validation and review requirements. Small PRs with a clear purpose are easier to review; there is no need to take on a whole subsystem. Please follow our [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Report suspected vulnerabilities privately through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), not in a public issue. ## License and citation Licensed under [Apache-2.0](LICENSE). For research using AgentScope, see [AgentScope: A Flexible yet Robust Multi-Agent Platform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14034).

items.description: Say what you want in plain words. Atris plans it, builds it, checks it, and shows proof. CLI plus MCP server, with project memory your coding agents share across sessions.
items.readme_text: # atris **atris**: you say what you want in plain words. atris builds it, checks it, and shows you proof. Under the hood it is an operating system for AI work. It turns any repo into a workspace an agent can actually operate: shared context it reads before it acts, a `plan -> do -> review` loop, durable tasks and daily logs, and verification that ends work on a real check instead of a promise. Every owner gets persistent computers to run it: ```text Owner = User | Business Owner has many Computers Computer = workspace + files + tools + secrets + memory + agents + validation loop ``` A computer can be personal or shared by a business. It can run a job like code, research, CRM, reporting, event ops, support, or business ops. ## Memory for coding agents Atris gives Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any other agent a memory that lasts across sessions. The memory is plain files in your repo: `atris/MAP.md` (where everything lives, with file and line numbers), `atris/wiki/` (what the team learned, as pages linked with `[[page-name]]`), `atris/logs/` (what was done and checked each day), and `atris task` (open work, who claimed it, and the proof). Every agent reads the same files before it acts, so several agents and people share one memory, reviewed in git like code. Mem0, Zep and Letta remember the users of a chat app. Atris remembers the project. Patterns and setup: [docs/agent-memory.md](docs/agent-memory.md). Comparison: https://atris.ai/blog/memory-for-coding-agents ## Check what ChatGPT can read about your business `atris aeo scan` checks whether ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and other answer engines can read your site. No login needed. ```bash npx -y atris aeo scan yoursite.com --vs competitor.com ``` You get a score out of 100, each gap with its fix, a side-by-side score against a competitor, and a draft `llms.txt` you can publish. To see what ChatGPT actually says when buyers ask about your business, run the free check at https://atris.ai/aeo/check. Guide to both checks and the tools that run them: [docs/answer-engine-checks.md](docs/answer-engine-checks.md). ## Quick Start ```bash npm install -g atris cd your-project atris init && atris ``` ## For Coding Agents **Read [`FOR_AGENTS.md`](FOR_AGENTS.md) first**: why agents adopt Atris, 60-second start, spread-it instructions. If you're an agent, run: ```bash atris ``` Then read the workspace's `atris/atris.md` and follow it exactly. `atris.md` is the source of truth. --- ## What Atris Gives You - An AI workspace on top of any repo - Persistent AI computers for scoped jobs - A local computer card that makes each workspace inspectable - A strict `plan -> do -> review` loop - Daily logs, task tracking, feature packs, and project memory - Skills, team members, integrations, and cloud sync when you need them - A plain answer to "what did my AI actually do?": run `atris recap`, or `atris recap --share` for a receipt-backed summary you can paste anywhere ## Critical Files | File | Purpose | |------|---------| | `atris/atris.md` | Main instructions for agents working in this repo | | `atris/MAP.md` | Navigation index with file:line refs | | `atris/TODO.md` | Human-readable task view | | `atris/logs/YYYY/YYYY-MM-DD.md` | Daily log, inbox, notes, completions | | `atris/features/` | Feature packs with `idea.md`, `build.md`, `validate.md` | | `atris/skills/` | Reusable skills for agents | | `atris/team/` | Team member specs and local context | | `atris/wiki/` | Repo memory, briefs, concepts, and wiki health | ```text atris/ ├── atris.md ├── MAP.md ├── TODO.md ├── logs/ ├── features/ ├── skills/ ├── team/ └── wiki/ ``` ## Install ```bash npm install -g atris atris --version ``` Requires Node.js 18+. `atris task` uses built-in SQLite and requires Node.js 22+. If you want Atris cloud workspaces, businesses, or integrations, run `atris setup` after install. ## How To Run Atris ```bash cd your-project atris init atris ``` `atris init` scaffolds the workspace, including `atris/wiki/`. `atris` loads context and hands the workflow off to `atris/atris.md`. If you're still shaping the idea, use `atris brainstorm`. If you want Atris to finish one job and prove it worked, use `atris run "<objective>"`. If you want Atris to keep picking the next mission or member until you say stop, use `atris autopilot`. If you want project memory checked for stale pages and missing context, use `atris loop`. `atris activate` surfaces wiki state from `atris/wiki/STATUS.md` when it exists. Core loop: `plan` -> `do` -> `review` Integrates with any agent. ### Publish a static site Upload any built static site to an Atris-hosted subdomain. See [docs/site-publish.md](docs/site-publish.md) for flags, limits, profiles, and troubleshooting. ```bash atris site publish dist --slug my-site --spa atris site publish . --slug my-next-app --profile app --build # Next.js static export ``` ### Bring people together with the Host The Host is a team member that gets to know everyone in a room (a company, a club, your own network) through one fun question at a time, keeps a card for each person, and introduces two people only when both say yes. Then it offers to find a time and checks that it happened. It never reads anyone's messages and keeps no scores. ```bash atris member install host atris host setup --room personal # your own network: it asks you, and drafts messages for you to send atris host import people.jsonl # bulk add people and who already knows whom atris host room # the host's weekly read ``` ### Put members to work Members are helpers that work in their own copy of the repo. Three words cover it. Run hands over one job. Atris picks the right member and starts it. ```bash atris member run "fix one failing test" ``` Wake keeps members working, each one pulling the next task that fits. Give a number, or name the members you want. ```bash atris member wake 5 atris member wake navigator executor ``` Wake only picks jobs that have a test to pass, so members know when they are done. Add one like this: ```bash atris task new "fix the flaky login test" --verify "node --test test/login.test.js" ``` Each job gets the time limit set for building in your roster, plus a few minutes for review. To see or change it: ```bash atris engine roster ``` Naming just one member runs one step of work. Add `--keep` to keep that one member working. ```bash atris member wake executor --keep ``` Sleep stops the members that are awake. ```bash atris member sleep --all ``` To watch them, open the board, or follow one member's steps as they happen. ```bash atris member board --watch tail -f ~/.atris/progress/executor.log ``` When a member finishes, ask for its result: what it changed, its receipt, and one number. Each member's copy of the repo stays until its work lands, then tidy puts it away. ```bash atris member result executor atris member tidy --dry-run ``` The older words still work as aliases: `dispatch` and `go` do what run does, and `up` does what wake does. ### How member work gets checked and lands Every member job ends with its own check, a command that must pass. Then a second engine reviews the change, and it is never the engine that did the work. Work lands on its own only after you switch self-landing on, once. From then on Atris pushes the branch, opens a pull request, and turns on GitHub auto-merge, so GitHub merges it when the branch is up to date and CI passes. ```bash atris autoland on ``` Anything else keeps the work on its branch, with one plain line saying why. That covers a failed check or review, unsaved changes, a clash with the main branch, and work that touches a protected area like payments, deploys, or credentials. A job that fails three times in a row stops and waits for a person. ## Chat With Atris 2 `ax` is the Atris 2 chat and coding-agent CLI. It uses the hosted Atris cloud by default, streams text, shows tool activity, and keeps fresh installs away from local setup. ```bash cd your-project ax chat ax --fast ax --fast "hello" ax --pro "help me plan this task" ax --max "reason through this hard decision" ax --doctor ``` Use Fast for quick chat and low-latency Atris loops. Use Pro for deeper tool loops. Use Max for the hardest jobs; it runs the highest-reasoning model and takes longer per turn. Advanced local workspace mode is opt-in with `--local` plus `AX_BACKEND_URL`. ## Play AgentXP AgentXP is the proof-backed game loop for getting better with agents. Start it inside any project folder: ```bash npm exec --yes --package atris@latest -- atris play ``` The first run creates a local starter mission if one does not exist. The loop is: ```text start -> proof -> accept -> login -> sync ``` The player path: ```bash atris play atris task claim <mission-ref> --as game-manager atris task ready <mission-ref> --as game-manager --proof "<artifact path + verifier result>" atris task accept <mission-ref> --as justin --proof "<human review>" atris xp card --local atris login atris xp sync --local ``` The manager path: ```bash atris gm --player justin ``` No proof, no AgentXP. `atris task done --proof` records review/RL context, but only human `atris task accept` mints Career XP for the local card or hosted leaderboard. ## Agents That Sign In On Their Own `atris login` signs a person in. An agent can sign itself in with an agent client, so no one has to hand it a login token. The owner makes the client once. The secret is shown one time, or written to a private file with `--secret-file`: ```bash atris agent-client create --name nightly-bot --scopes mcp:read,x-search --secret-file ./bot.secret atris agent-client list atris agent-client rotate <client_id> atris agent-client revoke <client_id> ``` The agent signs in with the id and the secret file. Its short token renews on its own; the secret and token are never printed: ```bash atris login --client-id atc_... --client-secret-file ./bot.secret ``` Or set `ATRIS_CLIENT_ID` plus `ATRIS_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE` (or `ATRIS_CLIENT_SECRET`) and run `atris login` once. It reads them, no flags needed, and opens no browser. After that every command renews the token on its own. `ATRIS_TOKEN`, when set, still wins. ## Business Owners If you want a shared owner for a company, lab, collective, community, artist, team, or project, use the business command instead of raw `atris init`. ```bash atris business init "Example Co" --owner-email operator@example.com cd ~/arena/atris-business/example-co atris business onboard --website https://example.com --contact "Example Owner" --note "sample customer workspace" atris align --fix ``` That creates the shared owner, creates its first/default computer, writes `.atris/business.json`, initializes `.atris/state/` for events and run history, and scaffolds the local `atris/` workspace under `~/arena/atris-business/<slug>/` with starter roles, a default recap template, and an initial task queue in `atris/TODO.md`. If you do not have a neat source pack yet, `atris business onboard` is the easiest intake step: give it a website, a named human, a few notes, or run it in a folder with loose files. Atris turns that into raw intake, a starter brief, a first workflow, a safe next action, and a short operator brief. Use the owner's language when you talk about it: ```text Your business runs on Atris. Your lab runs on Atris. Your collective runs on Atris. ``` You can also use bare input: ```bash atris business onboard https://example.com "founder-led b2b ops" ./notes.md ``` If you already have a folder full of source material, run it from there with `atris business init "Example Co" --here`. When the first recap is done, record it into the RL state logs: ```bash atris business record atris/reports/2026-04-12-operator-recap.md --outcome mixed --metric "operator speed" ``` ## Core Commands | Command | Purpose | |---------|---------| | `atris` | Load context and start | | `atris init` | Scaffold an Atris workspace | | `atris brainstorm` | Explore before planning | | `atris plan` | Create the plan/spec | | `atris do` | Execute work | | `atris review` | Validate work and capture learnings | | `atris run` | One bounded mission pursuit: start or resume, tick, complete (`--legacy` for the old plan/do/review chain) | | `atris run logs` | Browse glass run logs (phase reasoning persisted to disk) | | `atris run prune-logs` | Prune old run logs, keeping only the most recent N | | `atris run search` | Search phase reasoning across all run logs by keyword | | `atris run stats` | Show run log stats: phase counts, avg durations | | `atris run export` | Export all run logs as a JSON bundle | | `atris run diff` | Compare two run logs side by side | | `atris autopilot` | Keep the workspace moving: mission/member legs until `atris autopilot stop` (`--legacy` for the old approval loop) | | `atris pulse` | Install or run the durable overnight heartbeat | | `atris log "note"` | Add an inbox item to today's journal (`log --repl` for the editor; `wish` for headless intake) | | `atris now` | Show the current operating truth | | `atris radar` | Show live agents joined with tasks, missions, and worktrees | | `atris ctop` | Show process-first live agent CPU and memory | | `atris status` | Show active work and completions | | `atris task` | Durable local task state and the agent work loop | | `atris mission` | Durable goal, owner, verifier, tick receipts, and loop state | | `atris play` | Enter the AgentXP player loop for one proof-backed mission | | `atris gm` | Enter AgentXP General Manager mode for player missions and review queues | | `atris xp` | Show the local AgentXP card and sync eligible proof to the hosted leaderboard | | `atris codex-goal` | Inspect native Codex task goals and keep completed tasks closed | | `atris learn` | Manage structured learnings | | `atris ingest` | Stage raw evidence into `atris/context/` and compile into `atris/wiki/` | | `atris loop` | Refresh wiki health, stale/orphan signals, and next ingest candidates | | `atris wiki` | Full wiki namespace: ingest, query, lint, search, log, and loop | | `atris receipt` | Save evidence from an agent run | | `atris pay` | Pay another Atris account in credits (100 credits = $1); `history`, `show`, `accept`, `cancel` | | `atris trust` | See an account's trust and the friends you share; `vouch` or `unvouch` for someone | | `atris experiments` | Run small experiments and compare results | | `atris computer card` | Show or write the local owner/computer card | | `atris release` | Draft or publish a version bump, tag, GitHub release, and launch post | | `atris slop` | Deterministic slop detector: frontend/prose tells, plus `slop dead --exports` for dead code | | `atris clean` | Housekeeping: heal MAP refs, archive journals, report stale pages and dead code | ### Doctor `atris doctor [--json]` checks Node, task support, authentication, and workspace readiness. ### Document health `atris doc-health [--json] [--questions <path>]` scores document size, map coverage, lookup hops, and feature/member freshness from 0 to 100, and lists similar feature names. Tokens are estimated as characters divided by four. Boot load earns all 20 points at or below 80,000 characters, falls linearly to zero at 200,000, and stays at zero above that. Questions default to `atris/doc-health/questions.jsonl`, one `{"q":"where is the CLI router","expect":"bin/atris.js"}` per line. Custom paths are relative to the workspace root. Missing questions skip lookup scoring and contribute zero of its 30 points. Member age uses the newest log file's modification time. ## Built-In Systems - `atris learn` stores structured project memory in `atris/learnings.jsonl` - `atris wiki` keeps repo memory in `atris/wiki/` by default, with `--cloud` when you want the remote workspace path - `atris ingest` now stages local source packs under `atris/context/_ingest/`, writes a manifest receipt, and refreshes `atris/wiki/STATUS.md` plus `log.md` - `atris wiki --private` stores local-only sensitive notes under `.atris/presidio/` - `atris loop` refreshes `atris/wiki/STATUS.md` and `atris/wiki/log.md`, flags stale/orphan pages, and suggests the next ingest - `atris activate` loads the current wiki status so the next session starts with project memory, not just tasks - `atris member` keeps team-member identity and learning local-first: `MEMBER.md` is the role contract, `goals.json` is the machine-readable goal/experiment state, `goals.md` is the human readout, and `logs/YYYY-MM-DD.md` records what happened. Use `atris member goal`, `tick`, `status`, `block`, and `review <name> <experiment-id> --accept --proof "..." --value 1..5` to test whether a member is making useful progress or needs the operator/orchestrator. - `atris codex-goal` is the read-only bridge for native Codex `/goal`: `status` inspects the live goal database, while the legacy `reset` command now refuses every mutation. Active tasks continue in place; completed tasks retain their final goal, and new work or recurring monitors use a new dedicated Codex task. - `atris task` keeps durable local task state and append-only events for agents; `atris/TODO.md` is just a regenerated readable board. Run the loop with `atris task new`, `delegate "..." --to <owner>`, `next`, `say`, and `ready <id> --proof "..."`; human approval is `atris task accept <id>` (moves to Done, awards Career XP) or `revise <id> --note "..."`. Final task transitions also append the general daily log and, when a real `atris/team/<member>/MEMBER.md` matches the task owner, that member's daily log. Add `--json` for headless agents, `atris task serve` for the local board, and `atris task show <ref>` / `events --all` for the full ledger. The board prints a private link with a fresh token on each run and listens only on 127.0.0.1. Open that full link in the browser; API clients send its token in `x-atris-token` and use `application/json` for changes. Browser changes must come from the board's own origin. Commands accept semantic refs (`OBL-18`), full IDs, or any unique prefix. In cloud business workspaces, Supabase `tasks` is the source of truth and Swarlo the live claim layer. - `atris mission` is the durable autonomy layer: start with an owner, verifier, runner, and stop condition; record bounded work with `mission tick`; close with `mission complete` only after proof. Runners include `manual`, `claude`, `atris2`, and `codex_goal`. - `atris pulse` is the OS-cron heartbeat for overnight self-improvement. Use `atris pulse status`, `tick`, `run`, `install --cadence "<cron>" --days 7 --verify "npm test" --model claude-opus-5-5`, and `uninstall`. - `atris experiments` runs small test packs in `atris/experiments/` - `atris pull` and `atris push` sync cloud workspaces and journals - `atris live` keeps a business brain fresh by checking/fixing the workspace, pushing local state, pulling cloud state, and pushing again after local changes go quiet ## Engines An engine is the intelligence that builds a mission. Every installed headless coding CLI is a swappable worker behind one contract: a bounded prompt goes in, verified proof comes out, and engines never self-certify their own work. The house default is `atris-fast` (`ax`); `claude`, `codex`, `cursor`, `devin`, `grok`, and others join when their CLIs are installed. ### Who does each job `ROSTER.md` says which tool and model does each job. Edit it any time; every project, team member, and new chat follows it. ```markdown ## build - claude code, model: opus 5.5 ## review - codex, model: gpt-6-astra, effort: medium, max: 20 min, prep: search - claude code, model: opus 5.5 ``` The first ready worker leads and the rest are backups. `~/.atris/ROSTER.md` covers every project on the machine; `atris/ROSTER.md` overrides it for one project. A worker that stalls sits out 30 minutes and the next one takes over. The roster warns when a worker runs an old model and a newer one in the same family is on this machine, and prints the command that moves it. It also warns when a pinned model has no proof in 30 days. A landed run is proof; so is `verified 2026-09-30` on the line after a quick smoke test. ```bash atris engine roster # who does what, with each worker's recent record atris engine assign build claude --model "opus 5.5" # change a job's lead atris engine roster --available # tools and models on this machine atris team # who really worked in the last 7 days, then quiet and idle atris team --record # also save one row per member per day for the learning loop ``` Show every installed engine and the current default: ```bash atris engine ``` Flip the default for this workspace (persists to `.atris/engine.json`): ```bash atris engine cursor atris engine reset # back to the house default (atris-fast) ``` Ride a different engine for one run only, without changing the default. `--engine <name>` works on `mission run`, `autopilot`, and `run`. Per-run flags and `ATRIS_RUNNER_PROFILE` always beat the saved file. ```bash atris mission run "fix the flaky login test" --engine codex ``` ### Fleet Flight `atris mission run --fleet` staffs every idle installed engine on the board's claimable safe-lane tasks: one mission per task, one worktree per engine. Builds run in parallel; arrivals land serially with rebase-before-ship, so a rebase conflict pauses that landing (never auto-resolved) and keeps its worktree instead of orphaning work. Each flight writes a receipt to `atris/runs/fleet-<stamp>.json`. ```bash atris mission run --fleet --slots 3 # staff up to 3 engines atris mission run --fleet --dry-run # preview the staffing only ``` Each job goes to the builder its real results favor. The fleet counts what each engine landed and missed since Nov 1, on jobs like this one and on the rest (the same plays `atris rating` shows), gives every engine a fair chance, and prints the pick under the job with the numbers behind it. A landing counts only when its commit is on origin's default branch (the branch `origin/HEAD` names, never a guess), is no older than the claim it lands (five minutes of clock skew allowed), and no other claim recorded the same commit first: a commit counts once, for the first claim that recorded it, and not again for a later claim on the same job (reopened and claimed again, by the same engine or another) or for another job. That is judged on every landing record in the task store, in every workspace that shares it and every later review pass. A landing pays the engine that finished the job: when a stalled or dead engine's job is finished by another, the engine that finished it is credited, and a landing whose hand-in names several engines without saying which finished counts for none. The folder is judged in one order. With no git, no origin, or `origin/HEAD` not set (`git remote set-head origin --auto` sets it), no landing can be checked, so jobs are dealt in turn and the flight says why in one line. With an engine's landing on record, the flight fetches origin's default branch once before it picks (so a merge from a minute ago counts); if that fetch fails, jobs are dealt in turn with one line, and if it works the landings are checked. With only misses on record, they steer on their own, with no fetch. Everything git does before a pick shares one five-second budget and never prompts: its input is closed, `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT` is 0, and ssh runs in batch mode unless you set your own ssh command, which is left as it is and mentioned in one line. A play counts toward the kind of job it was when the engine took it: the claim, whether made by the fleet or by `task do`, saves the job's title and tags, so tagging or renaming a finished job later changes nothing, and a claim made before that was saved counts at half weight. New engines get tried; engines that keep missing get fewer jobs. An engine that is out of credit, cooling, or one the Claude spend guard would stop (a paid model nobody approved, or a pay-per-use key) is never picked, and the flight says which. The guard's own hook (`atris spend guard install`) stays the real guard on every unattended Claude run; this check only avoids picking an engine the hook would refuse, so where it is unsure it leaves Claude out. The fleet's own launch is judged by the `--model` the fleet itself passes, read through the `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL` remaps in the environment the worker will really get (a sealed one-lap worker gets none); with no `--model`, by `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` in that same environment, else the paid default. No Claude settings file is read, from any home. A custom launch template (`ATRIS_RUNNER_COMMAND_TEMPLATE`) is never read for its model, because a model in it can be a flag, a word of the prompt, another command's, or one the shell works out only when it runs. It counts as a model nobody can tell, which counts as paid, so Claude is left out with one line saying so, unless `ATRIS_CLAUDE_SPEND_OK` approves `default`; `--engine claude` still uses it. Your own choices come first and are never picked for, with results or without: `--engine <name>` sends every job to one engine, a job that names its engine gets it, and a job assigned to a member goes to that member's own engine, the same one `atris member` uses. A choice the flight cannot give is never given to someone else: a job that names an engine this flight does not have, or whose member's engine it does not have, is left out of the flight, with one line naming the job and why. It is taken out before the flight is staffed, so it takes no slot and holds no file against another job. The pick goes on who a job is assigned to and the engine it names, as the task list showed them; the claim asks the store for both again, inside its own transaction, and a job that now says something else is not claimed for the old choice. It is left for the next flight with one line, and the task list is drawn again so that flight reads the job as it is now. An engine list you name is never filtered, on the first pick or on a retry. If an engine dies mid-job, the next one is picked the same way; if it stalls and the roster lists a backup order, the roster's order stands. `--pick turns` (or `ATRIS_PICK=turns`) deals engines in turn, as before. ## Verifiable Feedback Loop Under the hood, Atris can keep score on real repo work. - Tasks can carry a `Verify:` command, so work can end on a deterministic check instead of pure prose. - Plan, do, and review now carry the same Confidence Gate: find every plausible loophole, patch it with source/proof/verifier/owner/rollback, or name it as residual risk before advancing. - `atris autopilot` can run that check after review and record the result in the journal. - Future task picks can use recent results, so Atris learns from repo-local history without claiming model retraining. ## Which AI Can Do Your Work `atris scorecard` measures which AI can do your team's work, on your own repo. ```bash atris scorecard # find past changes whose own tests can grade an AI (no AI runs) atris scorecard run # try each one with Haiku on your Claude plan atris scorecard run --models haiku,opus # compare models; past Haiku needs ATRIS_CLAUDE_SPEND_OK=<model> ``` - A past change becomes a task when its tests fail before it and pass after it. The ask is what your team wrote for that change. - The ask also names what the change's tests call that the change added or changed: a new file, a function with its arguments, an export, found with no AI. A good ticket names these; a commit message rarely does, and no model can guess a name nobody wrote down. - Each try starts from the change's parent in a throwaway copy with no remote. The change's own tests stay hidden until they grade the try. - Every try runs on your Claude plan login. Pay-per-use keys are removed, a try stops the moment Claude Code reports any other billing source, and nothing starts with extra usage on unless you pass `--allow-extra-usage`. - The scorecard shows how many changes each model did, how long it took, what the same runs would cost on pay-per-use, and which changes no model could do from what was written. - Tests that need their own command or settings go in `.atris/scorecard.json`. ## The Atris Rating `atris rating` gives every AI teammate one number, 25 to 99, for how much real work it finishes. ```bash atris rating # every engine the combine rated, and your members here atris rating opus # one engine's card atris rating <member> # one member's rating here, next to its engine's ``` - 99 means 99 of every 100 finished. Each halving of misses is worth about 6 points, so the top is the hardest climb: 3 in a row rates 76, and it takes about 60 in a row to rate 99. - Engines are rated in the combine: Loop Bench tasks from the atris repos, each graded by the tests that shipped with it. No engine is a 99 yet. - Each engine's card also rates its Python tasks, its JavaScript tasks, the tasks the Atris prompt was never tuned on, and how rarely a try broke another test, with its median time and pay-per-use price per finished task. - Members are rated on the same scale from the jobs they landed in your workspace over the last 30 days. Landed means accepted or merged; drops and abandons count against them. `atris gm` shows the same numbers. - When a person merges a builder's pull request, the builder is usually credited within the hour, by an `atris brief`, `atris rating`, `atris gm` or flight that reaches GitHub; `atris task sweep --held` does it right away. `ATRIS_HELD_SWEEP=off` stops the automatic check. - The session boot shows the build engine's rating, for example `build opus 5.5 (86 ovr)`. The combine grades building only, so review and search engines show none. ## Benchmark Harness Atris ships one public head-to-head benchmark harness for comparing a pinned single-model baseline against a coordinated stack run on the same task brief. Quickstart: ```bash node bin/atris.js experiments validate endstate-baseline node bin/atris.js experiments validate endstate-stack node bin/atris.js experiments run endstate-baseline --dry-run node bin/atris.js experiments run endstate-stack --dry-run node bin/atris.js experiments compare endstate ``` One-command rehearsal: ```bash node bin/atris.js experiments replay endstate ``` What to inspect: - receipts land in `atris/experiments/endstate-baseline/artifacts/` and `atris/experiments/endstate-stack/artifacts/` - scores append to each pack's `results.tsv` - `atris experiments compare endstate` prints the latest side-by-side comparison - `atris experiments replay endstate` runs the full public dry-run rehearsal - the benchmark contract lives at `atris/features/endstate/contract.md` - the verification log lives at `atris/features/endstate/validate.md` The stack wins Level 1 only if it beats the baseline on total score and does not lose the reviewed completion category. ## Skills Atris ships a real skill catalog in `atris/skills/`, not just one workflow file. Examples: - `atris`, `autopilot`, `autoresearch`, `wiki`, `loop` - `backend`, `design`, `copy-editor`, `meta`, `writing` - `github`, `email-agent`, `calendar`, `drive`, `slack`, `notion`, `slides`, `x-search`, `youtube`, `ramp` - `apps`, `create-app`, `create-member`, `memory`, `magic-inbox`, `improve`, `skill-improver`, `flow` ```bash atris skill list atris skill audit [name] atris skill fix [name] atris skill create <name> atris skill link [--all] ``` For Codex, copy any skill folder into `~/.codex/skills/`. ## Before a New Version Run the release-facing checks before bumping: ```bash node bin/atris.js --help node bin/atris.js pulse --help node bin/atris.js release --help node --test ``` Then dry-run the release: ```bash atris release --dry-run ``` `atris release` drafts or publishes from local git history. `--dry-run` prints the planned bump without committing, tagging, or pushing. ## Update ```bash atris upgrade # Install latest from npm atris update # Sync local workspace files to new version ``` Packaged npm installs check for new versions during normal commands and start a background update automatically. Git checkout installs stay manual so linked development copies are not overwritten unexpectedly. --- **License:** MIT | **Repo:** [github.com/atrislabs/atris](https://github.com/atrislabs/atris.git)

items.name: everruns
items.description: Headless durable agentic harness engine. Run durable AI agents reliably and scalably.
items.readme_text:
# Everruns [![Website](https://img.shields.io/badge/Website-everruns.com-blue)](https://everruns.com) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docs-everruns.com%2Fdocs-green)](https://everruns.com/docs) [![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/everruns.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/everruns) [![CI](https://github.com/everruns/everruns/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/everruns/everruns/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Repo: Agent Friendly](https://img.shields.io/badge/Repo-Agent%20Friendly-blue)](AGENTS.md) **Build capable AI agents in Rust. Run them where they belong.** Everruns is an open-source framework for building AI agents directly in Rust applications. Define agents, attach models and typed tools, run multi-turn sessions, and observe execution through one application-facing API. Use the framework in your application. When you need a shared runtime and production operations, run the Everruns platform yourself or use [Everruns Demo](https://app.everruns.com). [Build with the framework](https://everruns.com/docs/framework/quickstart/) · [Read the docs](https://everruns.com/docs/framework/) · [Try Demo](https://everruns.com/docs/getting-started/cloud/)

## Build an agent Add the application-facing crate: ```bash cargo add everruns --features openai cargo add tokio --features macros,rt-multi-thread export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... ``` Then define a typed tool, give it to an agent, and run a turn: ```rust use std::time::{SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH}; use everruns::{Agent, Engine, OpenAI}; #[everruns::tool] async fn current_time() -> Result { let seconds = SystemTime::now() .duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH) .map_err(|error| error.to_string())? .as_secs(); Ok(format!("{seconds} seconds since the Unix epoch")) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box> { let agent = Agent::builder() .name("assistant") .instructions("Use current_time when asked about time. Be concise.") .provider(OpenAI::from_env()?) .model("gpt-5-mini") .tool(current_time()) .build()?; let session = Engine::new().create(agent); let turn = session.send_and_wait("What time is it?").await?; println!("{}", turn.response); Ok(()) } ``` Everruns derives the tool schema from the Rust function, lets the model call it during the turn, and returns the result before producing the final response. [Continue the framework quickstart.](https://everruns.com/docs/framework/quickstart/) > **Note:** Everruns is under active development. Expect rapid changes and experimental features. ## The agent framework The [`everruns`](./crates/everruns) crate keeps the application-facing agent loop explicit and embeddable: - **Agents and sessions** — describe an agent once, then create independent, multi-turn conversations through an `Engine`. - **Models and providers** — start offline, use OpenAI, or attach a custom provider without coupling application code to a closed provider enum. - **Typed tools and capabilities** — give agents function tools and opt into filesystem, shell, web, Lua, and MCP boundaries deliberately. - **Events, cancellation, and lifecycle hooks** — observe a live turn, add application behavior at execution boundaries, and stop work cooperatively. - **Persistence and execution choices** — begin with engine-lifetime memory, add local crash-durable state, or cross deliberately into a distributed host. [Framework overview](https://everruns.com/docs/framework/) ## Choose how you run Everruns | Framework | Self-hosted platform | Everruns Demo | | --- | --- | --- | | Start here. Embed Everruns in the Rust application you are building; you own the process, deployment, integrations, and data path.

[Framework quickstart →](https://everruns.com/docs/framework/quickstart/) | Run the shared runtime in infrastructure you manage when you need a control plane, server, workers, UI, remote API, and durable execution.

[On your machine →](https://everruns.com/docs/getting-started/run-locally/) · [Docker Compose →](https://everruns.com/docs/getting-started/docker-compose/) · [Kubernetes →](https://everruns.com/docs/getting-started/kubernetes/) · [Architecture →](https://everruns.com/docs/explanation/architecture/) | Explore the hosted open-source platform with available promotional credit or your own provider keys.

[Everruns Demo quickstart →](https://everruns.com/docs/getting-started/cloud/) · [Try Demo →](https://app.everruns.com) | ### Platform capabilities The Platform, self-hosted or on Everruns Demo, adds durable execution, a stateless worker pool, a web UI, and a remote API. It also publishes agents to Slack, web chat, A2A, webhooks, schedules, voice, HTTP, and MCP; manages organizations and permissions; and supports observation, budgeting, and evaluation. [Platform capabilities](https://everruns.com/docs/features/capabilities/) · [Channels](https://everruns.com/docs/features/channels/) · [Durable execution](https://everruns.com/docs/explanation/durable-execution/) · [Observability](https://everruns.com/docs/observability/) ## Documentation Full documentation lives at **[everruns.com/docs](https://everruns.com/docs)**. - [Everruns Framework](https://everruns.com/docs/framework/) — build and run agents inside a Rust application - [Framework quickstart](https://everruns.com/docs/framework/quickstart/) — install the crate and configure a provider - [Run on your machine](https://everruns.com/docs/getting-started/run-locally/) — `everruns docker up` starts the full Platform in Docker - [Docker Compose](https://everruns.com/docs/getting-started/docker-compose/) and [Kubernetes](https://everruns.com/docs/getting-started/kubernetes/) — run it on a server or a cluster - [How-to guides](https://everruns.com/docs/how-to/) — give agents tools, stream events, publish to Slack, and enforce budgets - [API reference](https://everruns.com/docs/api/) — OpenAPI 3.0 - [SDKs](https://everruns.com/docs/features/sdk/) — Rust, Python, and TypeScript clients - [Docs as text](https://everruns.com/docs/llms.txt) — `llms.txt` index, per-topic Markdown sets, and the OpenAPI schema for agents ## Security Everruns runs untrusted agent and tool code for multiple tenants, so security is a core design goal. Threats are tracked with stable IDs across authentication, tenant isolation, permissions, tool execution, LLM integration, sandboxes, durable execution, and channel integrations, each with a documented mitigation and, where feasible, test coverage. - [Threat model](./knowledge/security/threat-model.md) — full analysis, mitigation status, and accepted risks - [Security testing](./knowledge/security/security-testing.md) — threat-model tests, failure injection, DeepSec scanning, and supply-chain checks - [Security policy](./SECURITY.md) — report a vulnerability ## How can I support this project? Everruns is a free, open-source hobby project. There are many ways to help: - Use Everruns and tell us how it went on [Discord](https://everruns.com/discord/everruns) or by email ([mykhailo@everruns.com](mailto:mykhailo@everruns.com)) - Report bugs and rough edges in [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/everruns/everruns/issues) - Star the repository, it helps other people find it - Write a blog post or share the agent you built - Help with the [documentation](https://everruns.com/docs/) by asking questions or sending PRs - Contribute code (see below, and say hi on [Discord](https://everruns.com/discord/everruns)) - Talk about Everruns around you ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) for local development setup and [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md) for the conventions used by both human and AI contributors. ## License MIT

One inbox. Every agent. All local.

The open-source workspace where Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode work from the same local Pages.

Website · Download · Changelog · 简体中文

## Install ```bash brew install --cask junyudev/tap/nodex ``` Or download [Nodex for Apple silicon](https://github.com/junyudev/nodex/releases/latest/download/Nodex-latest-arm64.dmg) and drag it to Applications. Nodex is in beta for macOS 15 and later. Sign in with the Codex, Claude Code or OpenCode account you already have — or start with OpenCode's free models. ## Why Nodex Coding agents are good at doing the work. Everything around it is still manual: turning a pile of ideas into prompts, choosing a model for each, remembering which chat owns which task, and getting the result back into your notes. Nodex does that part. Drop your thoughts into one Inbox and each becomes a Page with a plan: which Project, which agent and model, and what to hand off. The work runs in real chats with terminals, diffs and a browser beside them, and the results land in Pages that you and your agents both edit. Everything stays on your Mac. ## What makes it different ### One inbox that plans the work Drop in a burst of messages. In one pass Nodex suggests what to do with each: start a chat in the right Project with the right agent, model and effort; send it to a chat that's already on it; file it; or keep it as a note. A planned chat can name the parts its agent should hand to another model. Nothing runs until you confirm. ### Let Claude lead. Let GPT build. Any chat can hand parts of its work to another provider with `delegate_task`. A Claude Code session can fan out to GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex, keep an eye on every task, and merge what comes back. Each subagent keeps its own conversation you can open, follow up on, or stop. ### Bring the plans you pay for. Add the free ones. Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode are built in, and 40+ more agents install from the ACP Registry — Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, GLM Agent and others. OpenCode's free models sit in the same model menu. Usage meters show what's left of each plan, and the Inbox weighs it before it picks a model. Switch models mid-chat and your next message hands the conversation to the new Agent. ### The work lands in Pages you both edit Pages with properties, relations, sub-pages and history, organized in Board and List views. Every Inbox message is a Page that moves through Triage → Plan → Doing → Review → Done. Agents read and write Pages through the `nodex` CLI and Agent Skill, and attach reports, screenshots and traces as Page Files that open in a tab beside the Page, with HTML rendered in a browser tab. Their edits appear live in the window you have open. ### Ask once. Watch the whole board sort itself out. Your Pages and Databases live in one local Profile that agents can read and change in bulk. Ask in plain words. Behind the dock the agent runs the `nodex` CLI: one read-only SQL query over the backlog, then one atomic batch of edits that never overwrites newer changes. The View you have open regroups as it lands. ### Leave your desk. Not your agents. Nodex Mobile for iOS and Android reaches the computer your agents run on, and every team Space you belong to. See every chat, with the ones asking for you first; answer approvals and questions, queue a follow-up or stop a run; and drop thoughts into the Inbox, even offline. It connects directly over your local network or Tailscale, encrypted end to end, with no Nodex server in between, so it needs your computer on with Nodex open, or the team Space's host running. Turn on Remote access in Settings → Spaces, choose Link a device, scan the code, and [get the app](https://nodex.jyu.app/download/#mobile). ## Everything around the agent - **Worktrees and Environments** give each chat its own isolated checkout. - **Review** shows unstaged, staged, branch and last-turn diffs beside the chat. - **Browser, Terminal and Files** open next to the conversation that needs them. - **Scheduled** runs cron tasks and heartbeats on your Mac. - **Canvas, the command palette, split panes and multiple windows** keep a busy workspace navigable. - **Page history and whole-workspace snapshots** let you restore anything. - **Conversation import** brings your existing Codex and Claude Code chats along. ## Documentation - [Product specification](docs/product-specs/nodex-product-spec.md) - [Command-line interface](docs/CLI.md) - [Architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) - [Development guide](docs/development.md) ## License Nodex is open source under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE).

items.name: agentty
items.description: Agentic Development Environment (ADE) in your terminal
items.readme_text:
Agentty ADE

![NPM Version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/agentty) [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/agentty-xyz/agentty/graph/badge.svg?token=YRGKGTM0HP)](https://codecov.io/gh/agentty-xyz/agentty) [![Postsubmit](https://github.com/agentty-xyz/agentty/actions/workflows/postsubmit.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/agentty-xyz/agentty/actions/workflows/postsubmit.yml) [![Quality gate status](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=agentty-xyz_agentty&metric=alert_status)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/new_code?id=agentty-xyz_agentty) [![Bugs](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=agentty-xyz_agentty&metric=bugs)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/new_code?id=agentty-xyz_agentty) [![Code Smells](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=agentty-xyz_agentty&metric=code_smells)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/new_code?id=agentty-xyz_agentty) [![Duplicated Lines (%)](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=agentty-xyz_agentty&metric=duplicated_lines_density)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/new_code?id=agentty-xyz_agentty) [![Coverage](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=agentty-xyz_agentty&metric=coverage)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/new_code?id=agentty-xyz_agentty) Agentty is an **ADE (Agentic Development Environment) for structured, controllable AI-assisted software development**. Built with Rust and [Ratatui](https://ratatui.rs), and refined through its own day-to-day use, it brings agents, review, and iteration into one focused terminal workflow. [Installation](#installation) · [Supported CLI Agents](#supported-cli-agents) · [Usage](#usage) · [Documentation](#documentation) · [Contributing](#contributing) · [License](#license)
______________________________________________________________________ Codex, Claude, Gemini, and Antigravity sessions show compact tool status and command previews, with output previews for failed calls. Explicit Claude skill invocations appear alongside them, and answers retain saved usage counts. Press `w` in session view to inspect saved execution graphs, accept exact outputs, answer node questions, retry work, resume dispatch, or cancel a graph. With `--experimental-multi-agent`, `/graph ` generates an inspectable graph preview. `/graph query` shows its exact-version approval and cancellation commands; nodes launch only after approval. The `/plan` workflow uses bundled Markdown agent definitions. Repository overrides live in `.agents/agents//agent.md`; see the [workflow guide](https://agentty.xyz/docs/usage/workflow/) for the supported format. ## Installation ### npm (recommended) The `npm`, Bun, and `pnpm` packages require Node.js on your `PATH`. Global installs support automatic updates through the original package manager when Agentty can identify it. ```sh npm install -g agentty ``` ### Other methods
Bun ```sh bun add --global agentty ```
pnpm ```sh pnpm add --global agentty ``` If `pnpm` reports a global bin-directory error, run `pnpm setup`, reopen your terminal, and retry.
npx (run without installing) ```sh npx agentty ```
Shell ```sh curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/agentty-xyz/agentty/releases/latest/download/agentty-installer.sh | sh ```
Cargo macOS source builds require Xcode Command Line Tools for native process bindings. ```sh cargo install agentty ```
## Supported CLI Agents Agentty currently supports Codex, Claude, Antigravity, and Gemini. Install and authenticate at least one provider CLI before starting a session: - Codex (`codex`, recommended; supports subscription usage): install the [Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex) and run `codex login`. > [!NOTE] > > Codex is the recommended CLI agent for Agentty when you want subscription-backed > usage. Codex supports signing in with ChatGPT for subscription access, including in > the CLI, and Agentty uses the Codex `app-server` integration surface. Usage remains > subject to the [OpenAI Terms of Use](https://openai.com/policies/terms-of-use/). > OpenClaw documents ChatGPT/Codex subscription sign-in as the normal > [Codex harness](https://docs.openclaw.ai/plugins/codex-harness) path, and opencode > recommends ChatGPT Plus or Pro authentication for its > [OpenAI provider](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/#openai). - Claude (`claude`): install [Claude Code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code) and run `claude auth login`. > [!WARNING] > > For Agentty usage through `claude -p`, use API key authentication through Claude > Console or a supported cloud provider instead of a Claude Free, Pro, or Max > subscription sign-in. Anthropic's > [Claude Code legal and compliance docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance) > describe subscription OAuth as intended for ordinary use of Claude Code and native > Anthropic applications, while developer integrations should use API keys or supported > cloud providers. Theo's > [explanation video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RIkSlHgQYog) discusses the same > uncertainty, but commentary does not guarantee that subscription-backed usage is safe > for third-party tool invocation. - Antigravity (`agy`): install version 1.1.18 or newer of the [Antigravity CLI](https://github.com/google-antigravity/antigravity-cli) and run `agy` to sign in when prompted. > [!WARNING] > > For Agentty usage through `agy` headless mode, use authentication backed by a Google > Cloud project or an API key when available for your Antigravity setup, rather than a > Google Account subscription sign-in. The > [Antigravity terms](https://antigravity.google/terms) do not yet clearly describe how > subscription access applies when `agy` headless mode is invoked by third-party tools. - Gemini (`gemini`): install the [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) and authenticate with an API key or Vertex AI. > [!WARNING] > > "Sign in with Google" (Google Account OAuth) no longer works for the Gemini CLI after > Google's > [transition of the Gemini CLI to the Antigravity CLI](https://developers.googleblog.com/an-important-update-transitioning-gemini-cli-to-antigravity-cli/). > API key (`GEMINI_API_KEY`) and Vertex AI authentication still work, so use one of > those for the Gemini backend, or use the Antigravity (`agy`) backend instead. Agentty uses each provider's official non-interactive CLI or app-server surface (`claude -p`, `agy --input-format stream-json`, `codex app-server`, or `gemini --acp`) after you authenticate with that provider's CLI. It does not implement OAuth flows, read provider OAuth tokens directly, or call private provider APIs. You are responsible for choosing an authentication method that is permitted for your account, plan, and usage pattern. ## Usage Launch Agentty from the repository you want to work in. Project discovery is opt-in: the startup suggestion defaults to **Skip**, and the **Projects** tab supports adding a repository by path (`a`) or scanning a chosen folder (`d`). ```sh agentty # Launch with auto-update enabled (default) agentty --no-update # Launch without automatic updates agentty --otlp-endpoint http://localhost:4318/v1/traces # Export session traces agentty --experimental-harness # Offer preview Harness sessions agentty --experimental-multi-agent # Enable /plan and /graph agentty --help # Show supported command-line options agentty --version # Show the installed Agentty version ``` Start with `agentty --experimental-multi-agent` to enable `/plan`. Use it in a session with a prepared worktree, including a new **Regular** session, to turn the chat into a **Plan then implement** conversation. Answer or revise the read-only **Planner** proposal in the composer, then approve it in your own words to run the **Implementer**; follow-ups go to the Implementer. `--experimental-harness` adds a preview **Harness** session type that runs Agentty's built-in agent loop against a free local model, such as one a running Ollama serves, or against paid Muse, Kimi, or Qwen using `MODEL_API_KEY`, `KIMI_API_KEY` with `KIMI_BASE_URL`, or `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY` with `DASHSCOPE_BASE_URL`, or OpenAI's GPT models with a paid `OPENAI_API_KEY` or on your ChatGPT Plus or Pro plan after `ag-harness login chatgpt`. Its `/model` picker lists local models first, marks each model free, plan, or paid with a cheap, standard, or premium price class, and remembers your choice for new Harness sessions. A project's Default Fast Model can be a cheap harness model, such as `qwen3.8-flash`, for commit messages and titles. Its edit mode runs unsandboxed shell commands. See [Harness sessions](https://agentty.xyz/docs/agents/backends/#backends-harness). Session tracing is disabled unless `--otlp-endpoint` supplies a complete OTLP HTTP/protobuf traces URL. Authentication headers can come from `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_HEADERS` or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`. Traces contain step timings, tool identities, available executable names, exit codes, and output sizes. Add `--otlp-capture-content` to include tool commands, arguments, and results as previews of at most 4 KiB each. Common credential markers suppress the entire affected preview; arbitrary secrets may still appear. Prompts and reasoning are excluded. See the [session tracing documentation](https://agentty.xyz/docs/usage/workflow/#session-traces) for provider limitations. A traces URL ending in `/v1/traces` also sends the usage events below as OTLP log records to the sibling `/v1/logs` URL, even when PostHog telemetry is disabled. Only one Agentty instance can use a given Agentty root at a time. Close the running instance before launching another. Separate `AGENTTY_ROOT` directories can run independently. Telemetry is enabled by default: release builds send events to the Agentty PostHog project. Set `AGENTTY_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=0` to disable it. See the [telemetry details](docs/site/content/docs/usage/workflow.md#telemetry) for the exact events and fields. ## Documentation The programmatic session API supports creating and listing tasks before execution, submitting attempts, and explicitly accepting outcomes. See the [task contract](https://agentty.xyz/docs/core-components/durable-components/task/) for session ownership, concurrency, and current limits. It also supports explicit static execution graphs with isolated task conversations, exact output acceptance, and shared execution limits. See [execution graphs](https://agentty.xyz/docs/architecture/execution-graphs/) for supported profiles and lifecycle limits. Documentation for installation and workflows is available at [agentty.xyz/docs](https://agentty.xyz/docs/). > [!WARNING] > > Agentty is in active development. While releases follow Semantic Versioning, the > current `0.y.z` series may still introduce breaking changes between releases as > workflows, integrations, and safeguards evolve. Always review and verify the changes > Agentty proposes or applies in your repositories before you rely on them. ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for contribution guidance. ## License Apache-2.0

items.name: Coscribe
items.description: Coscribe is a local, user-friendly, highly agentic working assistant.
items.readme_text: # Coscribe [![CI](https://github.com/OICWS/coscribe/actions/workflows/office-agent-ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/OICWS/coscribe/actions/workflows/office-agent-ci.yml) A local, user-friendly assistant for office work. It reads and writes your files, produces Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF documents, makes Docs, slide decks, designs and dashboards you edit beside the conversation, uses the web and your tools, and can repeat work on a schedule. It needs only a model API key. Website: https://oicws.github.io/Coscribe/ - **Documents first.** High-quality `.pptx`, `.docx` and `.xlsx` output, checked by rendering the pages. - **Your models.** Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini directly, and any OpenAI-compatible API (DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, local runners). - **Connectors and skills.** Hosted services you sign in to once in your own browser, and skills (folders of instructions and files) you can read before adding. - **You stay in control.** Permission modes, approvals for risky tools, and per-tool settings for each connector. ## Run it ```bash cd office-agent python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 pip install -e ".[dev,web]" pip install -U "google-genai>=2.13.0,<2.14.0" cp .env.example .env # add a model API key (cd frontend && npm install && npm run build) coscribe-web # the web UI on http://127.0.0.1:8000 ``` [`office-agent/README.md`](office-agent/README.md) has the full setup and the features in detail. The Windows desktop app is built from [`office-agent-desktop/`](office-agent-desktop/). ## Repository | Path | | |---|---| | `office-agent/` | The Python backend, the React frontend and the tests | | `office-agent-desktop/` | The Electron desktop shell | | `docs/` | Engineering docs: the plan, decisions, the log of what shipped | | `site/` | The project website (GitHub Pages) | ## Contributing Developers and AI coding sessions: start with [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) (a map of the code and what to read first) and [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md). Before every change run `cd office-agent && bash scripts/check.sh`. Security issues: see [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md). Behaviour in the project: [`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). ## License [MIT](LICENSE)

items.name: AxioDB
items.description: Embedded NoSQL Database for TypeScript & AI Agents. Zero-native document database with ACID transactions & in-memory cache — verified on Node.js & Bun.
items.readme_text:
Embedded NoSQL Database for TypeScript & Agents

Zero-native embedded database with ACID transactions & in-memory cache — verified on Node.js & Bun.

[![CI](https://github.com/nexoral/AxioDB/actions/workflows/Push.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/nexoral/AxioDB/actions/workflows/Push.yml) [![OpenSSF Best Practices](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/16511/badge)](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/16511) [![OpenSSF Baseline](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/16511/baseline)](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/16511) [![OpenSSF Scorecard](https://api.scorecard.dev/projects/github.com/nexoral/AxioDB/badge)](https://scorecard.dev/viewer/?uri=github.com/nexoral/AxioDB) [![Known Vulnerabilities](https://snyk.io/test/npm/axiodb/badge.svg)](https://snyk.io/test/npm/axiodb) [![Socket Security](https://socket.dev/api/badge/npm/package/axiodb)](https://socket.dev/npm/package/axiodb) [![npm version](https://badge.fury.io/js/axiodb.svg)](https://badge.fury.io/js/axiodb) [![Zero native deps](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-0%20native-success)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/axiodb) [![ACID Durability](https://img.shields.io/badge/ACID-WAL%20Durability-blueviolet)](https://axiodb.in) [![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-6.0-blue)](https://www.typescriptlang.org/) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![GitHub Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/nexoral/AxioDB?style=social)](https://github.com/nexoral/AxioDB) 👉 **[Official Documentation — axiodb.in](https://axiodb.in/)**: full guides, API reference, and examples. This README is a quick start. ## Quick start ### Node.js & Bun ```bash npm install axiodb ``` ```javascript const { AxioDB } = require('axiodb'); const db = new AxioDB(); const users = await (await db.createDB('AppDB')).createCollection('users'); await users.insert({ name: 'Alice', age: 30 }); const { data } = await users.query({ age: { $gt: 25 } }).Sort({ age: -1 }).Limit(10).exec(); console.log(data.documents); ``` ### Deno (zero install via URL) No installation required in Deno — import directly via `esm.sh`: ```typescript import { AxioDB } from 'https://esm.sh/axiodb'; const db = new AxioDB(); const users = await (await db.createDB('AppDB')).createCollection('users'); await users.insert({ name: 'Alice', age: 30 }); const { data } = await users.query({ age: { $gt: 25 } }).Sort({ age: -1 }).Limit(10).exec(); console.log(data.documents); ``` No server to run, no `node-gyp`, no `electron-rebuild`. Requires Node.js ≥22 (also verified on Bun v1.4.0). ### 🤖 AI Agent Skill Building with Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Antigravity, or Windsurf? Install the official AxioDB skill so your AI agent generates verified query syntax, accurate transaction patterns, and avoids hallucinated APIs: ```bash npx skills add nexoral/AxioDB --skill skill ``` ## Why AxioDB? * 📦 **Zero Setup & Zero C++:** Pure JavaScript and TypeScript. No `node-gyp` errors, no build tools, and no native compilation issues on Node.js, Bun, or Electron. * 📄 **Native JSON (No SQL Migrations):** Store raw objects directly. Perfect for AI agents, chats, and apps where data structures change often and SQL schemas are painful. * 🛡️ **Safe from Crashes & Corruption:** Uses real ACID transactions and Write-Ahead Logging (WAL). Even if your app or server crashes mid-write, your data stays intact. * ⚡ **Fast In-Memory Caching:** Delivers sub-millisecond (<1ms) reads with a built-in memory cache and fast disk indexes. * 🤖 **AI-Ready:** Works out-of-the-box with AI coding assistants (Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot) via our official agent skill. ## When to Use It **Great for:** * **AI Agent Memory** — Save conversation history, tool calls, and agent state locally. * **Desktop & Electron Apps** — An embedded database that never breaks on user machines during updates. * **CLI Tools & Local Apps** — Save and query data easily without running a database server. * **Fast Prototyping** — Build full features with advanced queries without setting up Docker or cloud DBs. **Best fit:** 1,000 to 500,000 documents. **When NOT to use it:** * Millions of records, hundreds of concurrent web connections, or distributed clusters — use PostgreSQL or MongoDB instead. See [measured limits](https://axiodb.in/limitations). ## Features & Ecosystem AxioDB is designed to be **fully functional out of the box** with zero setup, while offering dedicated companion tools for advanced workflows. ### 📦 Built Directly Into the Core Package (`npm install axiodb`) Everything below is included in the main zero-dependency package — no extra servers, no Docker, and no native C++ compilation: * 🚀 **Zero-Setup Embedded Database** — Runs directly inside your application with `new AxioDB()`. No background database processes to install or manage. * 🛡️ **Crash-Proof Data Safety** — Incomplete writes roll back automatically if your app, server, or power cuts out mid-operation, ensuring your data is never corrupted. * ⚡ **Sub-Millisecond Reads (<1ms)** — Delivers blazing-fast queries with automatic in-memory caching and disk indexing, without needing to configure a separate Redis layer. * 🔍 **Rich Querying & Data Joins** — Filter documents with intuitive operators (`$gt`, `$in`, `$regex`), paginate, sort, and join multiple collections with aggregation pipelines (`$lookup`). * 🤖 **Built-in AI Agent MCP Server** — Pass `{ MCP: true }` to instantly boot an official Model Context Protocol server on port 27020, giving Claude, Cursor, and autonomous AI agents 45 tools to manage database state. * 🌐 **Built-in HTTP REST & TCP Servers** — Turn on `{ HTTP: true }` (port 27018) or `{ TCP: true }` (port 27019) whenever you need remote microservices, worker processes, or client apps to talk to the same database. ### 🛠️ Optional Companion Tools Install these only when you need dedicated standalone apps or command-line scripting: * 🖥️ **Desktop App (Electron GUI)** — A standalone desktop management application for Linux, macOS, and Windows to manage local and remote AxioDB instances without opening a web browser. * ⚡ **Terminal CLI (Go Binary)** — A lightweight, standalone CLI binary with an interactive REPL shell, TLS remote connections, and database backup/export/import tools. * 🤖 **AI Agent Skill** — Run `npx skills add nexoral/AxioDB --skill skill` to equip your AI coding assistant (Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, Copilot) with verified query syntax and schemas. * 🐳 **Official Docker Container** — Deploy `theankansaha/axiodb` in Kubernetes, cloud servers, or Docker Compose with all surfaces (HTTP, TCP, MCP) ready to run. ## Performance & Testing AxioDB is verified across **14 isolated test suites (329+ tests)** with a 100% pass rate, benchmarked at 100,000 documents on an AMD Ryzen 5 5500U / Node v26: | Operation | Latency | |---|---| | Indexed query | 1–2 ms | | `documentId` point lookup | <1 ms | | In-memory cache hit | <1 ms | | Range query ($gt/$gte/$lt/$lte) | 2–5 ms | | Sorted pagination (`.Sort().Limit()`) | 1–2 ms | | Insert single | ~31 ms | | Rollback | ~8 ms | Full performance charts, test suites, and methodology: [axiodb.in/performance](https://axiodb.in/performance). ## Tooling & Deployment ### Desktop GUI & CLI AxioDB ships an interactive Go CLI and an Electron desktop app for Linux, macOS, and Windows: **Linux / macOS:** ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nexoral/AxioDB/main/cli/Scripts/install.sh | bash ``` **Windows (PowerShell):** ```powershell irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nexoral/AxioDB/main/cli/Scripts/install.ps1 | iex ``` Prebuilt binaries are also available on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/nexoral/AxioDB/releases). ### Docker ```bash docker run -d --name axiodb-server \ -p 27018:27018 -p 27019:27019 \ -v axiodb-data:/app \ theankansaha/axiodb ``` All surfaces default to on, seeded with an `admin` account. See [Docker/README.md](Docker/README.md) for environment variables and configuration. ## Documentation | Page | Covers | |---|---| | [axiodb.in](https://axiodb.in/) | Documentation home | | [Create a database](https://axiodb.in/create-database) | Constructor options, collections, indexes | | [API reference](https://axiodb.in/api-reference) | Full method signatures and types | | [AxioDBCloud](https://axiodb.in/cloud) | Remote TCP access, TLS, authentication | | [Server API](https://axiodb.in/server-api) | The 41 HTTP endpoints | | [CLI](https://axiodb.in/cli) | Go CLI reference | | [Docker](https://axiodb.in/docker) | Image and environment variables | | [Security](https://axiodb.in/security) | RBAC roles, password policy, rate limits | | [MCP server](https://axiodb.in/mcp-server) | AI agent integration | | [Agent Skill](https://axiodb.in/.well-known/agent-skills/axiodb/SKILL.md) | AI agent progressive disclosure reference & runbooks | | [Limitations](https://axiodb.in/limitations) | Scope and measured limits | | [Comparison](https://axiodb.in/comparison) | Against SQLite, JSON files, lowdb, nedb, better-sqlite3 | ## Contributing, security & license Contributions are welcome — see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Security issues: report privately through [GitHub Security Advisories](https://github.com/nexoral/AxioDB/security/advisories/new). Policy details in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Author: Ankan Saha. Support the project with a ⭐ on [GitHub](https://github.com/nexoral/AxioDB) or through [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/AnkanSaha).

items.name: subshell
items.description: An agent / harness multiplexer that allows you to access your agents from any device and machine
items.readme_text: # Subshell Subshell is an open-source, self-hosted dashboard for interactive coding agents. Run Claude Code, Codex, and other agent CLIs on your own machines, then access them from a browser or desktop app. - **Your machines, your data.** Host the server yourself and run agents on its machine or enrolled nodes. You don't need a hosted Subshell account. - **Your choice of agents.** Built-in plugins support Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Cline, Open Interpreter, OpenHands, OpenClaw, Grok Build, OpenCode, Hermes, Oh My Pi, pi, a plain terminal, and SSH sessions. Add more through the plugin API. - **Work across devices.** Reconnect from a browser or desktop app, arrange sessions in workspaces, and share view or edit access with other users. - **Keep work together.** Browse workspace members and other subshells in one sidebar. Drag sessions in or out without stopping them, and follow subagents beneath their parent. - **Let agents coordinate.** The built-in MCP server supports cross-agent communication, encrypted channels, and helper sessions. ## Get started 1. Visit [Subshell downloads](https://subshell.sh) and install **Subshell Server** on the machine that will host your instance. 2. Open the app and follow the setup steps to install the server and create your administrator account. 3. Launch an agent from the dashboard. To run agents on another machine, install **Subshell Client** there and [enroll it as a node](https://docs.subshell.sh/get-started/another-machine). See [Install Subshell Server](https://docs.subshell.sh/install/desktop-server) for desktop setup, or [Installation](https://docs.subshell.sh/install) for CLI, Docker, and Proxmox LXC options. You can access the dashboard from a browser or [Subshell Client](https://docs.subshell.sh/install/desktop-client). ## Documentation The complete guides and references are at **[docs.subshell.sh](https://docs.subshell.sh)**. - [What is Subshell?](https://docs.subshell.sh/about): capabilities and reasons to use it. - [Get started](https://docs.subshell.sh/get-started): installation and access from other devices and machines. - [Use Subshell](https://docs.subshell.sh/guides): sessions, workspaces, and sharing. - [Server administration](https://docs.subshell.sh/administration): configuration, users, backups, and updates. - [MCP and agent communication](https://docs.subshell.sh/mcp): tools, channels, and coordination. - [Security model](https://docs.subshell.sh/concepts/security): protections, trust boundaries, and limitations. - [Developer guides](https://docs.subshell.sh/developers): plugins, API integrations, and contributing. ## Contributing Start with [Contribute to Subshell](https://docs.subshell.sh/developers/contribute) for development setup and verification. Contributions require the one-time [Contributor License Agreement](CLA.md). For work in this repository, [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) contains development instructions and links to notes for each app. The [engineering documentation index](docs/README.md) covers security rationale, release mechanics, the design system, and historical decisions. ## License Subshell is free to self-host and uses two open-source licenses: | Code | License | | --- | --- | | `apps/server/**`: the API, web dashboard, and server desktop app | [AGPL-3.0-only](apps/server/LICENSE) | | Everything else: the node, client apps, plugins, and shared packages | [Apache-2.0](LICENSE) | The server license includes an **API Type Surface exception**, allowing its TypeScript API declarations to be used under Apache-2.0. The exception covers types, not server implementation. See [the license text](apps/server/LICENSE) for its scope and terms. Subshell is copyright Disaresta, LLC. Commercial licenses for the control plane are available to organizations that cannot use AGPL-licensed software; contact [Theo Gravity](mailto:theo@disaresta.com).
